utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The interpreters are here. Good morning. Good morning to counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for the Defence, the accused. For the benefit of the public, I wish to say that we are in our last week, and we are listening, for the second day, to the closing arguments of the Prosecutor. It is still Mr. Kehoe, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. Mr. President, I would like to take us back to where we left off yesterday, and I just, before I move in through the rest of -- or continue on with my summation, I just, of course, would like to refer back and just reference exactly where we are. As I noted yesterday towards the latter part of the day, the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the ABiH, of course, reacted to the attacks by the HVO, and the reaction, as we will see in some of the coming evidence that we will discuss, was to shell the town and to begin an offensive. In fact, Blaskic's testimony reflects that the shelling was extremely intense on the 19th of April, 1993. In fact, upon review of these facts, Mr. McLeod, who, of course, wrote this ECMM report, which is Prosecution Exhibit 242, noted that: "The Muslim reaction from Zenica was to attack the key road junctions East of Vitez and North of Busovaca, effectively cutting off those two towns. The Muslim forces were only prevented from achieving this by accepting the intervention of the ECMM and UNPROFOR who brokered a cease-fire." So the 19th of April becomes a significant day, because at this particular juncture, the ABiH begins a rather strong offensive, and there are reactions by the HVO, and I will address those when we go back to the podium. The first such reaction, Mr. President, Your Honours, is the truck bomb incident that occurred on the 19th -- excuse me, that occurred on the 18th of April, 1993, but the more significant events occurred on the 19th of April; and that, of course, commenced with the Zenica shelling that took place in the midday of the 19th of April, 1993. Now, keep in mind, from Blaskic's own testimony, from his own comments and from the testimony of Slavko Marin and the reports that we have received from the Defence, there was shelling, heavy shelling, taking place on the 19th of April, 1993. What was the response of the HVO? The response from the HVO was the shelling of Zenica that took place in the middle of the day on the 19th of April, 1993. Mr. Hooper, with your assistance, if we could move to the next two photographs that are down below us? Mr. President, what we see are just two of a series of exhibits which reflect the carnage that was inflicted on downtown Zenica on midday of the 19th of April, 1993. These, as I say, are only two photographs of numerous photographs. I believe at this point, approximately 15 civilians were killed and numerous others were wounded. Mr. Hooper, if we can move to the yet third photograph in this regard? This is yet another photograph of the locale in downtown Zenica that the HVO shelled on the 19th. What is significant about this? It was shelling that took place in the middle of the day in a heavy civilian traffic area with no military targets in the locale where these shells hit the area and, of course, the predictable result occurred, i.e., the death and injury to numerous Bosnian Muslim civilians. What has been the reaction of the HVO and the immediate reaction of Tihomir Blaskic? Of course, as is predictable, "It wasn't us. It was the Serbs." Well, let's analyse that. Let's take this by a process of deduction and exclude the possibilities of who it possibly could be. Let us move, if we could, again with the assistance of Mr. Hooper, if we could take these documents down, and I will address the map that is on the easel, which is map 469. Mr. President, Your Honours, it is beyond any doubt that the shell that hit Zenica at midday, approximately midday, on the 19th of April, 1993, was a 122 shell. Major Baggesen testified to that. We had testimony from Witness W as well as a Bosnian Serb investigator, Judge Veseljak, who investigated that matter at the time. So we know that, in fact, a 122 shell landed in Zenica, or numerous shells landed in Zenica, killing those civilians. The question on the table is: Who fired that? Who fired the 122? Let's take this by a process of elimination, and let us examine this issue from the standpoint of the Defence witnesses. Early on in this case, the Defence called Blaskic's military intelligence analyst, an individual, now Brigadier Zeko -- I do believe, Judge Rodrigues, that might have been before you joined us -- but nevertheless, he was one of the early witnesses that was called by the Defence. In cross-examination by my colleague, Mr. Harmon, Mr. Zeko placed the artillery pieces belonging to the VRS, the artillery pieces belonging to the Bosnian Serb army. Where did he place them? He placed them at Location A and he placed them at Location B. These, of course, are the notations that were made by Brigadier Zeko. A follow-up question: "Brigadier Zeko, did the VRS have a 122 at either of these locations?" "No, they did not." Brigadier Zeko, the military intelligence commander, charged with knowing where enemy forces and enemy artillery is placed so he can advise Blaskic, testifies to this Chamber that there are no 122s in that location, either location. The next question asked by my colleague,

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "Tell us, Brigadier, what is the range distance between Point A, where the Serbs had an artillery piece, and Zenica?" His testimony is, 24 to 25 kilometres. Now, why is that significant? Twenty-four to 25 kilometres is significant because another - another - Defence witness, Professor Jankovic, the individual who testified on the angle of fire, said that such a distance was well outside the range of a 122. The simple matter was that from Point A to Zenica, you couldn't reach with a 122 shell. Let us move to Point B. Point B, the second point where the Serbs had an artillery piece, what is the range or what is the distance between Point B and downtown Zenica? Approximately 23 to 24 kilometres. Again, well outside the range of a 122 and, of course, as Brigadier Zeko added, they didn't have a 122 there anyway, "they" being the VRS. Where did the Defence witnesses testify that the HVO did have a 122? What was the locale? The locale that they picked was right here (indicating). This particular locale is Pucarevo. Now, from this particular location to downtown Zenica is the direction of fire that Major Baggesen, Witness W, and Judge Veseljak concluded from the splash marks was the direction of fire. Not this angle and not this angle, the angle from -- if I might point to it exactly? -- the angle of fire coming from approximately this location (indicating). Now, what else do we know from this particular location? We also know from this location that the distance between Zenica and this locale where the HVO had their 122 piece is somewhere between 16 to 18 kilometres, depending, if you move this mobile piece up and back. Now, this mobile piece, of course, as we have seen, is a piece that is taken from one location to another. It is carried around on the back of a truck. So when you place it at a particular location, after you fire it, according to Blaskic's own testimony, you don't keep that weapon in one locale, you move it around because, heaven knows, you don't want the enemy to key in on your artillery pieces by you keeping them there in an unsecured location for a significant period of time. But Marin tells us that, in fact, that 122 piece was located there. Now, there's been much debate about the angle of fire and the mathematics that Witness W took on the date when the shells actually hit Zenica, and that with the angle of fire as testified to by Witness W, Professor Jankovic said, "Oh, it is impossible for a shell to be fired from that locale with an angle of fire." Let's assume that Witness W made a mistake on his field mathematics that he took that day. Let us take us to the next question. Mr. Cayley asked Professor Jankovic, "Professor, if we had approximately a four-degree discrepancy, a four-degree error in that angle of fire, could that shell have reached?" What was his answer? "Yes. Yes." The shell could have reached from this location if the mathematics was four degrees in one direction, and certainly if that weapon had been moved up it could have reached as well. So what do we have? We have field calculations that -- based on what Witness W said are possibly erroneous, but with an adjustment of approximately four degrees the weapon could, in fact, reach there, the 122. We know, based on Marin's testimony, the chief of operations and at that point the deputy chief of staff of Blaskic, that, in fact, they did have a 122 at that location, and we know that the VRS did not have a 122 within range. The weapons that they did have were out of range and, in fact, those weapons weren't 122s at all. Now, assuming that the Bosnian Muslims didn't shell themselves and murder their own civilians, which nobody has made that argument, the only conclusion is, and the conclusion of independent third parties on the ground such as the British Battalion, was that the HVO fired on Zenica on the 19th of April, 1993, and in a moment we will answer why. The answer why, Mr. President and Your Honours, finds itself in the rationale given to this Court by Lieutenant-Colonel Bryan Watters, then Major Watters, the second in command of the Cheshire Regiment as part of the British Battalion. What did he tell us? On page 3409 -- now, mind you, this is at a time when the Bosnian Muslim offensive, the ABiH offensive is under way. What did Watters testify to? He said:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because shelling Zenica was going to achieve no tactical advantage to the forces in retreat into Vitez and Busovaca, HVO forces, against the onslaught of the BiH, and we could only assume that the HVO had fired their artillery into Zenica as a warning to the Muslim forces to stop attacking. Now, that is a rationale that was made on the ground by Major Watters, in the British Battalion, in and around the 19th of April, 1993. They rejected Blaskic's explanation that the VRS had actually shelled Zenica, and concluded that the HVO had done it, and they concluded that they did it by saying, "If you continue this offensive, we are going to shell your cities and we can reach your civilians." Now, the question that comes up: Is this an isolated incident? Is this the only time that such an effort was conceived of and thought about by the HVO command and Blaskic? The answer is it is not. This event took place on the 19th of April, 1993. Let me take you up just several months in the chronology to the Stari Vitez and Vitez attack on the 18th of July of 1993. You recall Blaskic's testimony that on the 18th of July, 1993 Darko Kraljevic and others conducted an offensive against the ABiH and, of course, the ABiH responded. After that particular offensive by Kraljevic or the HVO was under way and then the ABiH responded, the ABiH was successful in repelling that attack. On the 20th of July, 1993, while the ABiH counter-offensive was under way, Darko Gelic makes a very interesting comment to Captain Lee Whitworth, the liaison officer of the British Battalion. Of course, Captain Whitworth is in the second generation of the British Battalion, part of the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire. But before we talk about that comment, let's ask a question. Who is Darko Gelic? Darko Gelic is Blaskic's hand-selected liaison officer to the British Battalion and to international agencies. This is Blaskic's man who goes out and takes care of business and passes on information for Blaskic. What does Gelic tell Whitworth on the 20th of July, 1993? Because what he tells him is very, very probative of what the HVO intended on the shelling of Zenica on the 19th of April. On the 20 the of July, 1993, and this is in Exhibit 711, P711, Darko Gelic says this: "Darko Gelic, the three Op zone HVO liaison officer claimed that if the ABiH attacked Vitez, then the HVO will retaliate by shelling Zenica." Now, I submit to you, Your Honours, does anyone suspect that Darko Gelic came up with that strategy on his own? That he would tell the liaison officer for the British Battalion that the HVO would shell Zenica in July if he hadn't consulted and spoken with Blaskic? I submit to you no. That strategy, that strategy of curtailing any BiH offensive was well ingrained in Blaskic's thinking and within the HVO. They had two cards in the deck that they were prepared to use if an ABiH onslaught took place. Actually, three. The first one, of course, is the shelling of Stari Vitez, which we will talk about in a few moments, which they did. The second one, of course, is the blowing up of the Vitez factory, which, of course, Blaskic threatened to do, in documents that we've seen. The third, and the one that we've seen repeated both in April and in July, is the threat against the town of Zenica and the civilian population in Zenica. There is no doubt that based on these three events that the strategy of Blaskic, in order to curtail the ABiH offensive into Vitez, is clear. One of the prongs that he was prepared to use and, in fact, on the 19th did use was the shelling of Zenica, a purely terrorist, criminal act designed to accomplish one specific goal, and that is to send the ABiH a message and that message is, "If you come in here we're going to get your civilians and we can reach them." If I may, before we move to the next topic, I would reflect on one point concerning the actual use of artillery, and I think that Your Honours have to keep in mind that the use of artillery, barring smaller pieces that were designated to the brigades, the use of artillery by Blaskic's own testimony was under his sole command and control. Let us move on. Mr. President, Your Honours, one can not look at the particular event in Zenica and the shelling of Zenica in isolation, because many things happened. Numerous things happened on the 19th as attempts by the HVO to curtail the ABiH offensive. One of those most significant events and the most serious threat at this time was the threat that was conducted on the evening of the 19th to the 20th of April, 1993. That is later on, on the same day as the Zenica shelling, 19th of April, 1993, Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic, was brought to the cinema building. The cinema building which is, of course, not only the place where civilians are incarcerated and from which they're taken out to dig trenches, but it's also, it's also the headquarters of the Viteska Brigade and Mario Cerkez. What happens that evening? Cerkez brings Mujezinovic in and, of course, Mujezinovic is not only a physician, he's also a political leader in Vitez, and he makes a series of threats to him. Cerkez, in the presence of Zvonko Cilic and various other members of the HVO, brings Mujezinovic in and says, "Do you know what happened in Ahmici?" Mujezinovic says, "Yes, I'm aware of what happened in Ahmici." He says, "What I want you to do," and this is Cerkez speaking, "What I want you to do is go downstairs, get other leaders from the Bosnian Muslim community, and call 3rd Corps, and call Sarajevo, and call anybody you want and get them to stop the offensive. Get them to cease the ABiH offensive. And if you don't do that, I will kill the 2.225 civilians that we currently have in custody." Now, when does this threat take place? This threat takes place outside the back door of Blaskic. By our estimates, it's approximately a one-minute walk. By his estimates, it's approximately a 40 to 50 minute walk -- a 40 to 50 metre walk. These civilians, where this threat is taking place, is essentially in his backyard. Now, not only is Cerkez making this threat, but Blaskic's colleague and a person who he gets along with very well and consults with, Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak, also make that same threat in the early morning hours of the 20th of April, 1993. I believe the record reflects it's somewhere in the area of 05.30 or approximately 06.00 in the morning that Santic and Skopljak come back in and make the same threat. Ivo Santic is, of course, the mayor of Vitez. Pero Skopljak is an HVO leader and HDZ party official. Just a reference back, Pero Skopljak is the individual that I spoke about yesterday, who, on approximately the latter part of October 1993, noted at a press conference that the HVO is the only authority in Vitez. Nevertheless, in their efforts to engage this cease-fire, what, in fact, do they do? They force Dr. Mujezinovic to sign a document. If we could move to the next exhibit? What we see here, Mr. President, Your Honours -- I'm not sure Your Honours can see this, but this is Exhibit 86, French on this side and the English on the right-hand side -- what we see is a compulsion by the HVO, Santic and others, to force Muhamed Mujezinovic to sign a document compelling him to what? "4. Both sides agree that in Vitez and Province 10, the Vance-Owen Plan should be implemented --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. Can we please have the text on the ELMO? I do admire you for the big exhibits that you have made, but I think it would be advisable for the benefit of the public to have these documents on the ELMO. Never mind then. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can put the French copy on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No. The interpreters don't have the text either, I am told. I am asking -- I can understand that the registrar cannot have all the exhibits at hand; it would take a lot of time. You have taken care, and I thank you for it, for these very large exhibits. When it is a map, we can see it on our monitor. So I don't see why this document cannot also be shown. It would allow the public to follow the debate more easily. I think this is a possible improvement that we can make, but we are not going to interrupt you, and please continue now, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to assist the public and to assist Your Honours, we have put the French copy on the ELMO. We can flip back with the French and the English, as need be. Hopefully that will be of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. That's very well like that. Thank you very much. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, let us go back. What do we see, Mr. President, Your Honours, in the midst of these combat operations? What do we see are the desires of the HVO? We see once again their desire to implement the Vance-Owen Plan. At the possible threat to 2.225 civilians and other individuals in custody, they want to implement the Vance-Owen Plan in their canton. That is the overriding concern. What do they say? "Both sides --" and this is point 4. "4. Both sides agree that in Vitez and Province 10, the Vance-Owen Plan should be implemented even before it is signed by the Serbian side. Also, the army commands shall retain their structure in conformity with the ethnic composition of the province and the municipality." Again, laced through everything that is going on within the HVO is the political and military desire to implement this plan in this canton. That explains in large part the effort that is taking place militarily on the ground that commenced on the 16th. Of course, this counter-offensive by the ABiH that is conducted on the 20th didn't subside, and there are a sequence of events of exactly what transpired on the 20th. Now, contrary to the testimony of the accused, the shelling continued on the 20th. He has testified that there was very little shelling on the 20th, and there is a good explanation as to why he decided to lie about that because of what exactly he and other members of the HVO did during the 20th and the use of human shields. Nevertheless, let us analyse his particular contention that there were no human shields. What was taking place on the 20th? The 20th saw yet another day in the counteroffensive by the ABiH of shelling of downtown Vitez. How do we know that? We know that, first and foremost, from Exhibit 187. That is three exhibits up, 187, which is an ECMM report. In this report dated the 20th of April, 1993, in point 3, ECMM wrote: "3. Ceasefire - Violations (unconfirmed). T34 tanks --" T34 being an old JNA-style tank. "-- were told to be in positions on the mountain road between Zenica and Vitez. Shelling HVO HQ and the PTT building in Vitez. HVO is said to be putting an ultimatum on Gacice, and after that failed, HVO is said to have started attacking the village." If we can just go into private session just briefly, Mr. President, to refer to another small bit of testimony in this regard? (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think we can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. What was Blaskic's response to this continuous shelling in downtown Vitez on the 20th of April of 1993? If we can take a look at the exhibit that is on the ELMO, that is an exhibit that is a portion of Exhibit 45. What it depicts are three locales. Location A is the Hotel Vitez; Location B is, of course, the cinema where the prisoners were being kept and also Mario Cerkez's headquarters; and Location C, to the left of the letter "C," is the communications centre or the PTT building. If you recall from the ECMM report that we just discussed, on this same day, the HVO had completed their attack on Gacice and had subdued Gacice, and from the testimony that Your Honours have heard, they took civilians and put them in various houses, I think it was approximately seven houses, in Gacice. What happens later on in the afternoon on the 20th of April? Two hundred and forty-seven civilians, 247 civilians are brought to downtown Vitez and are told to sit in the space next to the Hotel Vitez. If Your Honours view the ELMO, the overhead that is on the ELMO, the area that is circled and is designated number 1 is the area that was circled and designated by a witness, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: (redacted) testified that the HVO soldier that brought them down makes a comment that, "Well, you know, now you're going to see what it's like to have people shell you." But more importantly, he says that, "I am going to come in and tell the commander that you are here." Now, who is the commander in the Hotel Vitez on the 20th of April, 1993? Who is the person who is in charge on the 20th of April, 1993? Certainly not Mario Cerkez. That's not his headquarters. It is Blaskic's. It is Blaskic's headquarters. He testified to Your Honours that he was totally unaware of this gross violation of international humanitarian law. But interestingly enough, who was aware of it? His then acting deputy chief of staff and his chief of operations, Slavko Marin. Slavko Marin knew that those individuals were there. What did he tell us? On page 13554:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's talk about these women and children that were taken back to Gacice. Because after they successfully acted as human shields around the Hotel Vitez, they were taken back to Gacice and stuffed back into several houses. I will continue on with this testimony:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in downtown Vitez before they were taken back to Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Gacice is right next to the town of Vitez, and as far as I know, these civilians were in town, and I cannot say what the exact location was, I cannot say at this point. However, the town of Vitez is not a very big town, so it could have been between the post office, the municipality building, the cinema building, et cetera. So he knows that these people are down there. Of course, Blaskic denies it. His right-hand man, the person he is operating with, stuck in the basement on these two telephones knows about it, but, of course, Blaskic does not. Because, of course, if he knew something about it, he would have to do something about it; and even if he found out after the fact about it, he would still have to punish somebody because of it, and, of course, he never stopped it because he knew about it, and even if he did know about it, no one was ever punished. It goes on:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, on the 20th of April -- And this, I'm sorry, is page 13565:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, on the 20th of April did any member of the HVO come into the Hotel Vitez and tell you or Colonel Blaskic or any other officer in the headquarters that women and children were outside the Hotel Vitez at this location that is circled in Exhibit 158, the one that's on the ELMO? Did any soldier do that? Very interesting response by Brigadier Marin:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that, but I know that out of those civilians who were brought in, none were killed and none were wounded that day. That I do know. So he doesn't know about the individual soldier coming in to tell him that they're there, but he knows, he knows, that nobody was told and none of those people that were surrounding the Hotel Vitez were killed or injured that day. How does he know that? How does he know that? We are talking about a very small geographic area several metres away from the main headquarters where Blaskic is in charge. Both Marin and Blaskic knew full well that those civilians had been brought out there, knew full well the strategic and tactical reasons why they brought those civilians and surrounded the Hotel Vitez with those civilians on the 20th of April, 1993. I will note for Your Honours that during this offensive, this is the only instance in the entire war where civilians are brought to the Hotel Vitez. The only time. Two hundred and forty-seven civilians brought as human shields. The only time. And Marin knows about it and Blaskic does not. I submit to you he lied and shaded the truth significantly in this regard once again because the consequences for Blaskic, of course, bring with it criminal sanctions. Let us continue on, because as we continue on we probe yet deeper and examine Blaskic's total disregard for the civilian population and for individuals who are ordered to combat or outside of combat and thereby should be protected under the Geneva Conventions. Where were the civilians and other individuals who were out of combat incarcerated commencing on the 16th of April, 1993? Two very interesting locations. At the Dubravica school and at the cinema building. The Dubravica school, up toward the front line, is not only the place where these individuals were incarcerated, individuals, civilians that were taken from Ahmici, and Santici, and Nadioci, for instance, but it is also the headquarters of the Vitezovi, a legitimate military target for any counter-offensive by the ABiH, and Blaskic knew that. Where is the second, and for the purposes of our discussion, a much more interesting location because of its proximity to his headquarters? The second locale where hundreds of civilians were being kept at various times is the cinema building. You recall the testimony of various witnesses that some of these prisoners were in the basement and it got too crowded and some people went back up to the cinema building. This is the same cinema building that is approximately one minute away, by walking, from Blaskic's headquarters. The cinema building is also the same location that is Mario Cerkez's headquarters. It's also known, for the purposes of our discussion, as the Workers' University. If we can move to these photographs, if we can, on the easel. This is a similar photograph to the one that we viewed before. This is, again, a portion of Exhibit 45, and again, just for clarity's sake, "A" is the Hotel Vitez and "B" is the building that is both the cinema and what they call the Workers' University. It is a building that is connected, that has a figuration of a "T", if you will, with the Workers' University being the top of the "T" and the cinema building being the bottom part of the "T". Clearly, artillery fire directed at this legitimate military target, which it was, would have placed in serious jeopardy the numerous, the numerous civilian -- Bosnian Muslim civilian detainees who were being incarcerated in the cinema building from which, of course, and we will talk for a moment, hundreds of them were taken to dig trenches all throughout the area of the Lasva Valley. Now, Blaskic knew two things very, very well. He knew the Geneva Conventions, and he knew the Protocols, and he knew what was a violation of the laws or customs of war, and he knew those things that were not. He was aware, when I asked him on cross-examination, of provision of Article 51(7) of Additional Protocol 1, which reads in part: "The presence or movements of the civilian population or individual civilians shall not be used to render certain points or areas immune from military operations, in particular in attempts to shield military objectives from attacks or to shield, favour or impede military operations. The Parties to the conflict shall not direct the movement of the civilian population or individual civilians in order to attempt to shield military objectives from attacks or to shield military operations." Now, he was aware, by his own testimony, he knew that those civilians were in the cinema building. He testified he knew at least on the 17th. He actually knew on the 16th, but he knew, by his own testimony, that they were there on the 17th. He knew that putting them in harm's way to protect a military target was against the Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols. He was also aware that the Workers' University had been the subject of attack. How did he know that? Let us turn to Exhibit 327, Defence Exhibit 327. If we look at first -- actually it's the second full paragraph. "Around 16.00 from the region of Vjetrenica, probably from the road, saddle Vjetrenica-Kuber, Muslim forces shelled the town area of Vitez from a tank, (probably T-34). The municipality building was hit, and the enemy was probably targeting the buildings of the Post Office, the Hotel, Workers' University as well as civilian facilities in town." Now, this is a report that he received on the 19th of April, 1993, that Marin testified came from the Viteska Brigade. So he knew they were there on the 17th. He knew it was a violation of the law, and he knew that the Workers' University was a target of attack. And what does he say? "I couldn't do anything about it. I had to wait for the ICRC to come in and take their names down. I had to keep them there in harm's way. I couldn't do anything about it. I couldn't move these civilians to another locale. I couldn't move them to a safer location. That would have been a violation of ICRC's rules and regulations." I submit to Your Honour, he never, ever, ever gave that explanation to a member of the ICRC, and I defy any ICRC individual to come forward to say that, "We were against taking civilians to safer areas, to places that were out of harm's way." These people were in there on the 17th, at least by his own testimony on the 17th, and they didn't begin to get released until the 30th of April of 1993, and some even after that, into the first week of May. All that time, both in the Dubravica school and in the cinema building, they were in harm's way and subject to attack on legitimate military targets, and what did Blaskic do about it? Nothing. Nothing. He took no steps whatsoever to protect those civilians who were in harm's way. We have been focusing, of course, for most of our argument on the cinema, but obviously the same argument concerning not taking these civilians out of harm's way pertains to the numerous civilians from Ahmici and other villages around Ahmici that were incarcerated and detained in the Dubravica school. Now, let us move on to the next egregious crime committed by Blaskic and the HVO, and that is the pervasive, the ever-pervasive and continuous pattern going back until at least January and continuing throughout the HVO campaigns in April and, of course, again in June, and that is the trench digging that Bosnian Muslim detainees are forced to conduct. Blaskic, by his own testimony, was informed, was informed on the 5th of February, 1993, in a meeting at which General Merdan participated that Bosnian Muslim detainees were being forced to dig trenches. He was told, on the 12th of February that two Bosnian Muslim detainees, told to the ICRC, by the way, a woman by the name of Iris, he was told that two Bosnian Muslim detainees taken out to dig trenches had been murdered. He says they were punished. He couldn't answer some very significant questions in that regard, the first one being, "What punishment did they receive?" and the second one being, "Were they removed from the HVO permanently?" He didn't know. What we do know as regards that significant event that he admits Bosnian Muslim detainees were killed, is that the commanders in Busovaca, such as Dusko Grubesic, were never dismissed or removed from command as a result of this practice, never. And guess what happens in April? Predictably, when Blaskic gives the order to begin to dig trenches, a written order drafted by Slavko Marin that goes out to the brigades, what happens? Brigades and all units, excuse me. The brigades comply with that order, and there is written responses back from both of those brigades to Blaskic, that the Defence has submitted into evidence, that the trench lines have been dug. How have they been dug? Through the forced compelling of Bosnian Muslim detainees to dig those trenches. A witness testified to this Court that in February of 1993, every man, woman, and child in Busovaca knew that Bosnian Muslim detainees had been taken to dig trenches. It was such a massive practice that everyone knew. Of course, except Blaskic. He's in communication with his people in Busovaca but he doesn't know. History repeats itself predictably. In April of 1993, where the practice becomes yet more massive than that which was undertaken in February, hundreds of Bosnian Muslims are taken and forced to dig trenches. Detainees are forced to dig trenches. Taken from the Kaonik camp, for instance, taken from the cinema building about 30 or 40 metres away from his headquarters, taken from the Dubravica school, taken from the veterinarian station and the SDK building, all being taken to dig trenches. And what's Blaskic's explanation? He don't know nothin' about nothin'. That's nonsense. There is a key rationale as to what the HVO is all about, and the rationale that was set forth by the warden of the Kaonik camp, Zlatko Aleksovski explains exactly what the HVO was doing when they were forcing these Bosnian Muslims to dig trenches. If I could, if I will, Mr. Hooper, if you could put this chart back up on the easel. This, of course, Mr. President, is again part of Mr. McLeod's report, the ECMM report that he took in May, 1993. It is part of Exhibit 242. What we have done is blow up a portion of the interview that Mr. McLeod conducted with Zlatko Aleksovski, the warden of the Kaonik military prison, and what does he say? He is complaining to Mr. McLeod about various incidences. He says: "The 5th is the kind of work that the prisoners have to do because I know that the Geneva Conventions do not allow prisoners to be taken for any work if their lives are in danger. I have been warned about that by the ICRC as well. "But I am not the only one responsible for this because I just carry out orders. The brigade commanders in Busovaca and Vitez give them. Not that I really want to avoid my responsibility, because I am not the one who releases people to do the work. In order to clear it up, I went with Beatrice of the ICRC to the commander in Busovaca, where she protested for the people to be taken to work under such conditions. "She was given the answer I almost completely agree with. We here actually do not have enough people to do the security jobs. Somebody has to dig the trenches, and it happened that the men to do that were the prisoners. On the contrary, it would happen that Busovaca would be occupied. I do not need to explain what would happen if Mujahedin occupied it. So in a way, the Muslims protected Busovaca." So here we have direct subordinates of Blaskic, his two brigade commanders in Busovaca and also in Vitez, going to Kaonik camp and taking Bosnian Muslim detainees out to dig trenches throughout the area. This is not a work platoon. This is not some work detail that has been set up by the defence department as Blaskic testified about. It's nothing like that. These are detainees that have been taken out to dig trenches, and the reason given by Aleksovski is the reason employed by Blaskic, "We need to dig trenches. We don't have enough soldiers to dig these trenches, so we are going to use these detainees." That's the reason, a very cold, rational reason, which also happens to be a violation of International Humanitarian Law. The trench digging, of course, Mr. President and Your Honours, was pervasive and continued. It didn't take place just in the Vitez area. We need only go to the testimony of Father Pervan, another Defence witness. Father Pervan was a Defence witness who testified about numerous things. Father Pervan was a priest, a Catholic priest from the Kiseljak area. What was going on in the Kiseljak area? What was taking place in Kiseljak was the same thing that was taking place in the Lasva Valley, and that is the forced -- or forcing Bosnian Muslim detainees and civilians to dig trenches. I think the view or the explanation given to Father Pervan is instructive, because it parallels that which was given by Zlatko Aleksovski in May of 1993, and I am reading Father Pervan's testimony at 14523:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, trench-digging I consider to be wrong, just as I consider the war to be wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever raise concern, the concerns that you had, with the HVO command in Kiseljak about the use of Muslim men for forced trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke about that, and I received the following answer, "We need trenches in order to remain, and let them dig it. We give them cigarettes and alcohol. Nobody is mistreating them or beating them while they are doing this work, and so, they are not, they are alone. The Croats are there, too, and they are escorted." That was the answer that I heard several times. The testimony that Your Honours heard, of course, throughout this trial, is that civilians that were on the front lines digging trenches were, in fact, beaten; and civilians, Bosnian Muslim detainees that were forced to dig trenches, were, in fact, killed while they were performing this ever-dangerous work. And the explanation given by Colonel Morsink and the rationale given by Colonel Morsink as to why the HVO did this is instructive and compelling. The HVO forced Bosnian Muslim detainees to dig trenches on the front line for one reason: It was dangerous. It was very dangerous. Colonel Morsink reasoned that they forced them to do this because it would put them in harm's way and they wouldn't expose their own personnel and their own soldiers to that danger. That's the reason they did it. And no one was ever punished for this practice, what once began in earnest in April of 1993, and no one was punished, disciplined, sent to gaol, dismissed as a result of this practice; and lo and behold, if we move ahead yet again several months to September of 1993, we see Blaskic doing the same thing: compelling Bosnian Muslim civilians to dig trenches on the front lines. If we could turn to three exhibits that we addressed towards the end of Blaskic's testimony? Those exhibits are Exhibits 715, 716, and 717. This is a series of documents that we addressed towards the end of Blaskic's cross-examination, that he, of course, did not tell the truth about until he was shown these documents, and the first one is a document that is dated the 10th of September of 1993 that reflects on the third full paragraph -- if we can go up with that, Kirsten -- and this deals with the forced work units: "Two members of the work unit were killed while at work and two were wounded." I will not read the entire document, but I would like to turn to the last page of this document. I would like Your Honours to keep in mind that Blaskic testified on direct examination that he never took or never had individuals going to front-line positions to dig trenches. That, of course, was before this document was shown to him. This is a document, of course, that is written on the heels of the Grbavica offensive that Blaskic conducted on the 7th and 8th of September of 1993. The Grbavica feature was taken by the HVO forces on September the 8th, 1993, and this document reads as follows. If we can focus in on that top paragraph? "On 8 September 1993, a verbal order was issued by Colonel Blaskic to engage a minimum of 100 people from the work units to work on the consolidation and digging-in on the first defence lines on the Jardol-Divjak-Grbavica axis towards Sadovace." The bottom line in that paragraph: "The remaining personnel are to dig in at the first defence line." Now, this is an order by Blaskic putting these work units on a front-line position; not in some back-line position to dig trenches, not in some back-line position to dig dugouts. This is an order that is given immediately after the combat in Grbavica ends. These are first-line trenches on the front line that Blaskic sends them to. And lo and behold, look what happens? If we go to the bottom part of that paragraph, the bottom part of the last paragraph. "Some members of the second group were abused and beaten by some soldiers which can be established on the basis of statements of the commanders of the work unit." "Beaten and abused" in September of 1993. I ask Your Honours to hearken back to the testimony of numerous witnesses from April and May of 1993 who were beaten and abused while being forced to dig trenches on the front line, and I ask the question once again that keeps coming back, because it is inescapable, as to what would have happened to these individuals who were killed or beaten and abused in September had Blaskic punished somebody, punished just somebody for beating or abusing or killing a Bosnian Muslim detainee who was forced to dig trenches in April of 1993? He didn't do it. He didn't do it because he didn't want to do it. And as a result of that, he signalled to his troops that this was okay, and, in fact, he ordered them to go to the front lines, which, in fact, they did. The next document, and we will take 716 last, the next document being 717, reflects a series of individuals which are clearly Muslims by their names, although Blaskic says they're Gypsies, Muslims all being forced into work platoons. And the last document that I would like to talk about is a document on the 20th of September, 1993, which again, in accord with the verbal request of Commander Tihomir Blaskic, yet more individuals are taken to a front-line position to dig trenches. If I may for one moment, Mr. President, before we complete this document before the break, I would just like to go into private session on Exhibit 716. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in. Please be seated. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Prosecutor, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President and Your Honours, the next issue to be addressed is, of course, in addition to the burnings and killings we have any number of expulsions of the Bosnian Muslim population that took place throughout the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. By Blaskic's testimony himself, in approximately March of 1993, approximately 60 per cent of the Muslim population wanted to depart the Kiseljak municipality. One need only ask the question: "Why?" But that displacement and expulsion of the Bosnian Muslim population, of course, increased in earnest after the commencement of hostilities on the 16th of April, 1993. We need only take a case in point of what happened to those civilians from Gacice, those civilians that we were talking about earlier today that had been taken and placed around the Hotel Vitez, which of course Blaskic knew about. What happened to those civilians when they returned to Gacice? Were they permitted to conduct their lives as normal? Of course not. They were kept in approximately seven houses, jammed together, and then ultimately they were taken on trucks by the HVO and taken, as so many other Bosnian Muslims that we've heard about, they were taken to the mountain road going to Zenica, taken to a checkpoint and told to walk across no-man's land and walk into Zenica. How many of those individual Muslims were expelled? I need only recall the testimony of Sefik Pezer, one of the individuals who lived actually in the town of Vitez itself. After he was expelled from Vitez, he had occasion to visit the Red Cross facility in Zenica. He was told of thousands, and he met any number of those individuals who had been expelled from the Vitez area during the time frame commencing on the 16th of April of 1993. Blaskic knew about this, and his knowledge and his failure to do anything about it was pursuant to an organised plan. If I may briefly go into private session in this regard, Mr. President, I would appreciate it. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's continue now, please, in public session. Please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As we move into May, Mr. President, Your Honours, we see a reduction in the hostilities in the Lasva Valley area and an eruption of those hostilities and attacks by the HVO in other locales, specifically in Mostar. As of the 9th of May, 1993, the HVO attacked the city of Mostar, and that encirclement and siege of Mostar remained in place until, I believe, approximately the 27th of February of 1994. Of course, in that instance, as in others, thousands of Bosnian Muslim civilians were detained and numerous Bosnian Muslim civilians -- hundreds of Bosnian Muslim civilians were killed. While we move into June, a different sequence of events transpires. The tide begins to change in Central Bosnia. We begin to see, in June of 1993, an offensive taking place by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the area of Travnik. The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina successfully takes Travnik. The offensive that is going on at the same time is an offensive that takes place down in the Kiseljak area, where the attacks take place in villages such as Han Ploca, Tulica, and other areas in that locale where the Bosnian Muslims are attacked by HVO forces operating in conjunction with the VRS, with the Bosnian Serb army. This is a very interesting development, as we look at the timing of it. Now, Blaskic would have you believe that he saw very little of Kiseljak during this time frame. That is, of course, not the case. We, of course, direct the Court to the testimony of Brigadier Duncan, who notes that he and the other British Battalion brought Blaskic to Kiseljak on the 29th of May, 1993, initially for a meeting at the U.N., which was very brief and meaningless, according to Brigadier Duncan. And thereafter, Blaskic, with Milivoj Petkovic and Ivica Rajic, go off to the Kiseljak barracks for a meeting and meet for several hours, through the balance of the business day. As we move into June, we see a sequence of events in various locales involving the Bosnian Serb army and the HVO, and the common thread in all of those locales is Blaskic. In mid June, we see the VRS, as I noted -- I'm talking about the 12th and 13th of June -- the VRS and the HVO attacking Bosnian Muslim villages in Tulica and Han Ploca together with the VRS offering artillery support in those villages. As with so many others, we have the time-honoured tradition of killing civilians and non-combatants, burning of homes, destruction of mosques. In the Travnik area, we have HVO soldiers moving, who were retreating, moving through VRS lines with civilians, in through the civilians, and if we look at an exhibit such as Exhibit 744, a document that comes from the Krajina Corps, the commander the Krajina Corps notes, in pertinent part: "You may provide fire support for HVO forces in requested areas." So in and around the locale in Travnik, the HVO is participating with the VRS, and that's not the only locale. There is combat ensuing up in the Zepce area. In the Zepce area, the HVO is again operating in conjunction with the VRS in attacks against the ABiH. Now, the question to be raised is: Who is the commander in Zepce and Travnik and in Kiseljak? Who is the common person? Certainly not Ivica Rajic. The common person and common commander is the defendant Blaskic, and I will note that in a document that the Defence put in evidence, which is an interview of General Alagic, General Alagic refers to conversations and communications that Blaskic was having on regular bases with VRS commanders on the Vlasic feature. Nevertheless, as we move on, we again have the time-honoured tradition in the attacks in June of 1993 in Kiseljak where civilians are detained, they are again beaten and abused at the school in downtown Kiseljak as well as the Kiseljak barracks, and those individuals are taken relentlessly to dig trenches throughout the area. As of the 16th of June, there is a cease-fire, a tripartite cease-fire, and after that, a joint command is set up, which we will talk about at another juncture, where Blaskic and Hadzihasanovic meet with Brigadier Duncan and Ambassador Thebault to discuss the protection of the civilian population, and if Blaskic didn't know that all these civilians in Kiseljak were being abused prior to these meetings, after those meetings on the 19th, the 21st, and the 28th of June of 1993, he certainly knew then that civilians were still being arrested, that civilians were still being taken out to dig trenches, that the Kiseljak mosque was destroyed, et cetera. Of course, consistent with this prior conduct, nothing happens. In response to all this, as we move into July, we have the interesting attack of the 18th of July, 1993, on Stari Vitez. What did Blaskic tell us about Stari Vitez? He testified that this was an attack that was conducted solely by Darko Kraljevic and the Vitezovi and it was contrary to his orders and he didn't know anything about it until he got back to Vitez at 1800 hours and the entire time he was down with the priest from Busovaca, going to mass and having lunch, and he was totally unaware of the day's events. Interesting story, but, of course, it's not true. How do we know it's not true? We know it's not true from the account of exactly what transpired, and I turn Your Honours' attentions to Exhibit 708, and 708 is a military information summary that chronicles what transpired on the 18th of July, 1993; and contrary to Blaskic's testimony where he allegedly was criticised for not giving artillery support to the HVO troops, let us read what the British Battalion, that was on location at the time, noted. "On the 18th of July at 0045 in the morning --" 0045 in the morning. "-- an intense barrage of the Muslim area began and involved occasional multi-barrel rocket launchers and artillery fire as well as mortars, and the fighting has continued throughout the day." There is a commentary by Darko Gelic, the ever-present Darko Gelic, who is Blaskic's liaison officer. I ask the Court to look at this comment that Darko Gelic gives to Captain Whitworth, in light of Blaskic's testimony that he doesn't know anything that's taking place in this attack. Darko Gelic, the Operative Zone Central Bosnia liaison officer to BritBat has confirmed that the HVO are attacking Stari Vitez and that the artillery barrage was the preliminary phase. Now, how does he know that? How does he know that this artillery barrage, commencing at 0045 -- artillery which, by the way, is under the control of Blaskic -- but how does he know that this artillery barrage is the initial phase of an attack? If he is Blaskic's liaison officer, he's not even supposed to know it's going to be taking place. It defies logic. Gelic knew that the artillery attack was taking place and that it was a preliminary phase because that was the plan. That was the plan that Blaskic ordered and that was the plan that was undertaken. Likewise, this is not only Darko Kraljevic and the Vitezovi that received casualties as a result of this. If we examine Exhibits P758 to P763 as well as the actual death reports that the Defence put in, D345, we see individuals killed from the Viteska Brigade, the Vitezovi, as well as the military police, and I believe that Exhibit 345, the Defence exhibit, also puts individuals from Tvrtko II, another special purposes unit, in the fray. So this was hardly an attack that was taking place merely with the Vitezovi; it was a coordinated attack by various units of the HVO that are operating at the same time in concert with artillery support, as most military operations that take place undergo: First an artillery barrage, and then an offensive barrage by these four units. To argue that Blaskic is the only person that didn't know this was going to happen and that it did happen is simply not true. All these units and their unit commanders knew about it, Blaskic's LO, liaison officer, knew about it. What does the Court have to conclude? That he knew about it. He knew about it too. What he doesn't want to admit and he doesn't want to admit and the reason he doesn't want to admit that he was involved in this operation to subdue Stari Vitez once and for all: because it was a massive attack on a civilian population. It was not only a massive attack on a civilian population that was also used, it was an attack that was indiscriminate in its nature. If you would put the next exhibit on the easel, Mr. Hooper, which is a ... What is this, Your Honours? This is a photograph of something that is called a "baby," and what this is the outside of a fire extinguisher that is stuffed with fertiliser, benzene or some type of accelerant, petrol, and it is launched and fired. What is the problem with this particular piece of weaponry or ordnance, if you will? You can't direct it. It fires indiscriminately. If Your Honours examine the testimony of Captain Bower that was led by my colleague, Mr. Cayley, he will tell you how these things actually -- what direction they fire in when they land. They can't be guided. They can be given a general direction, but you don't know exactly when they're going to come down and where they're going to come down. Why? Because aerodynamically, they're not attached with the type of fins that we normally see on ordnance that is put on a mortar shell or is even put on a bomb that is sent out of a bomber. In any event, it is a type of ordnance that is totally indiscriminate. And what Blaskic and his troops did was fire hundreds of these things into Stari Vitez over the course of the war, many, many, many of which were fired on the 18th of July of 1993. What does Blaskic know? Blaskic knows full well that firing such a type of ordnance into a civilian-populated area is a crime. So he can't tell you he was there. And that's why, that's the reason why he says he's down in Busovaca and knows nothing about an operation about which his liaison officer is fully informed. I will note, Mr. President and Your Honours, this is the same liaison officer, if I might remind the Court, who, two days after this attack on Stari Vitez, noted that if the ABiH offensive continued, that they were going to attack Zenica. The next sequence of events that we move into, Your Honours, goes to Grbavica, the attack on the town of Grbavica, the feature next to the British camp that took place on the 7th and the 8th of September of 1993. What do we know about that particular attack? We know several things about that attack from Blaskic's own testimony. We know first and foremost that he planned it. He, with his commanders, selected the troops. He was the one who was out on the ground examining this operation while the entire matter was under way. There's no allegation that he was in the basement of the Hotel Vitez, there is no allegation he was at church in Busovaca or home in Austria or down in Grude. He was there when this took place. Who did he employ for this combat operation? Well, certainly he employed members of the Viteska Brigade and certainly there were members of the Vitezovi involved as well. You only need look at Exhibit 250 where the Vitezovi acknowledge that they were, in fact, involved. Of course, when this particular attack was conducted, nobody in the Vitezovi was ever punished, disciplined, dismissed, or anything else for crimes such as the truck bomb. Who else was involved? The 3rd Light Assault Battalion was involved. And who is the 3rd Light Assault Battalion? The 3rd Light Assault Battalion is the second generation of the Jokeri, the military police unit that had conducted the atrocities and were involved in the atrocities in Ahmici. Let me just take you back and just take you briefly through the course of events. The Jokeri existed through approximately the latter part of July of 1993 and early August. From Blaskic's own testimony, the 4th Military Police Battalion was taken over by Marinko Palavra, (redacted) (redacted), and they established an anti-terrorist unit called the 3rd Light Assault Battalion, and the members from the Vitezovi became part of the 3rd Light Assault Battalion. Now, when Lee Whitworth examined the soldiers that were involved in this Grbavica attack, he recognised these soldiers as members of the Jokeri. In addition to that, Palavra conceded that the 3rd Light Assault Battalion or the Jokeri were probably involved in Grbavica because his guys were not involved. Last but not least, we know that the 3rd Light Assault Battalion of the military police were involved because Pasko Ljubicic, in Exhibit P357, three years a military police, says so, that they were involved as a combat unit in Grbavica. What happened in Grbavica was similar to what happened in numerous other locales. The take-over and the initial attack on Grbavica was a legitimate attack; it was a legitimate military objective. It was a place at which the ABiH had had positions and were denying access along the road to the HVO. So there was no question that Blaskic had a legitimate reason for attacking that feature. But it is not the attack on the feature that is the crime, it is what happened thereafter and some of the methods that he employed while he was in there. After these particular locales were secured, what happened was the HVO soldiers burnt the houses, looted the houses and ultimately the entire village was burnt. If we could move to the next series of photographs. If you recall the testimony of Captain Lee Whitworth concerning this event, Captain Whitworth went down to Vitez while the attack was under way on the 8th of September, 1993. In the transcript or in his testimony he notes various pieces of interesting information. On his way back shortly after lunchtime, while the attack was still under way, he drove back towards Grbavica and he examined the skyline which was burning. I believe we have another photograph that also depicts that, Mr. Hooper. This is a similar photograph, of Captain Whitworth, taken on the 8th that also depicts the burning of Grbavica. Now, contrary to Blaskic's statement, Captain Whitworth said the houses were burning before the attack ever finished. What Blaskic testified to was a handful of houses were burnt while the combat was under way. Put that in stark contrast to the testimony of Captain Whitworth who that said that that was simply not the case. Houses were burning and burning during the course of that day. What happened after that? If we could move to the next several photographs, Mr. Hooper. Again, this is another photograph of HVO soldiers. This one, of course, carrying a radio that he looted from one of the houses. Let's go to the last photograph. Yet another photograph of HVO soldiers carrying looted weapons. This is 433/24. Again, a different soldier carrying a radio which he obviously looted from the location. So what we have is burning of houses after the HVO had successfully secured the feature, burning houses that was totally unnecessary, sending, of course, as Captain Whitworth noted, the message to the Bosnia Muslims, "Don't return to Grbavica." They looted those houses and certainly looting took place by the civilian population thereafter. One item I forgot, during the course of this testimony, that was employed by the HVO, that Blaskic forgot to mention, and that is the next photograph, which is a photograph 433/28, a photograph taken by Captain Whitworth, which is a baby in mid flight, being launched onto the houses in Grbavica. So in this operation that Blaskic plans, they use illegal, unguided ordinance to attack homes, and we have that in a photograph taken by a Captain of the British Battalion while the weapon was in mid flight. We thereafter have the time-honoured tradition of HVO soldiers securing premises, burning the houses unnecessarily. Of course, not necessary militarily. And last but not least, the looting of the houses thereafter. What, of course, do we then know after that? We then know that on the same day Blaskic, the 8th of September, 1993, Blaskic orders that civilians be taken to front line positions just the other side of Grbavica to begin digging front line trenches. So if we look at this particular operation that Blaskic himself planned, his crimes are numerous. Using illegal ordinance, permitting his soldiers to burn Bosnian Muslim houses and directing their attack against Muslim houses contrary to any military necessity, the looting of those houses and, of course, forcing civilians, Bosnian Muslim civilians to dig trenches on front line positions, and this, by his own testimony, is an operation that is planned by him and him alone. Suffice it to say it was all predictable. He uses the second generation of the Jokeri, he uses the Vitezovi, all these units that he said he's complained about in combat operations, knowing full well what they had done in the past, knowing full well what they were capable of, and lo and behold they repeated their conduct yet again. So we come to an end of this portion of the final argument before I turn the floor over to my colleague Mr. Cayley. The bottom line in all this, Mr. President and Your Honours, is that when all is said and done, by the latter part of 1993, there were virtually no Muslims left in Vitez, in the area controlled by the HVO. No Muslims left in the area controlled by the HVO in Busovaca and fewer Muslims still in Kiseljak, in the area controlled by the HVO, except possibly in the village of Rotilj which had been described by the UNHCR as a concentration camp, where hundreds of Muslims were stuffed into that little village. The Muslims were gone. The plan had worked, they had been evicted from the area, and the tool implemented that policy was the accused Tihomir Blaskic. I can only hearken back to the comment Franjo Tudjman made to the Right Honourable Paddy Ashdown on the 6th of May of 1995, when Ashdown asked Tudjman what was to become of the Muslims and the Muslim state, and Tudjman responded, "There will be no Muslim state." That was the plan, that was the design, and that was what Blaskic was sent to the Central Bosnia Operative Zone to do. I thank you at this point, Your Honours. I don't know, with the schedule, if should we turn the floor over to Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. In principle, we should continue until 1.00 and, of course, it is up to the Judges to give the floor to the next speaker, and we welcome him. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. My task in the closing argument is to address you on the special legal and evidential requirements in those counts in the indictment which are charged under Article 2 of the Statute, the grave breaches provisions. I will address you both on the most recent law of the Tribunal and the evidence presented in this case pertaining to those counts, and they are Count 5, wilful killing; Count 8, wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury; Count 11, extensive destruction of property; Count 15, inhumane treatment; Count 17, taking civilians as hostages; Count 19, also inhumane treatment but in respect of conduct which is discreet when compared to the evidential foundation for Count 15. If I could first of all hand out a binder. My production is a rather more low-budget affair than Mr. Kehoe. I don't have any large photographs to show you. I've gathered some exhibits which I think should be brought to your attention, and I've prepared a file for each of you and for the Defence. They are not in the order in which they were admitted into evidence, so I've tabulated them, and I'll refer to the tabs along the side when addressing you on the particular exhibit. What are the special legal requirements or ingredients which are a prerequisite for the application of Article 2? Most recently, they have been enumerated in the judgement of the Appeals Chamber in the Dusko Tadic case, and I would refer you to paragraph 80 of the Appeals judgement. The requirement is twofold. The conflict between the parties must be international in nature. The second requirement is that the grave breaches must be perpetrated against persons and property defined as protected by any of the four Geneva Conventions of 1949. Let me address you on the first requirement, that the conflict between the parties must be international in nature. In a case such as the instant case before you, where the Defence assert that there was an internal armed conflict taking place between the Bosnian Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, I would submit to you that there are two primary areas of consideration for you. The first is this: What legal conditions must be met to demonstrate that the HVO were acting on behalf of the Republic of Croatia? The second consideration is whether in this case the evidence adduced satisfied those conditions. What are the legal conditions that must be met? The Appeals Chamber has recently confirmed that the proper test to establish whether the control of Croatian authorities over the HVO -- and I'm inserting "Croatian" and "HVO", the test was, of course, stylised in a generic fashion -- whether or not the control of Croatian authorities over the HVO was sufficient to make the armed conflict be international is overall control, going beyond the mere financing and equipping of such forces, and involving also participation in the planning and supervision of military operations. That you will find in the Tadic appeal judgement at paragraph 145. Has the evidence adduced in this case satisfied those conditions? My submission to you is that it has in overwhelming fashion. The evidence supporting the assertion that the HVO were de facto agents of the Republic of Croatia can, in my submission, be neatly divided into Croatia's political ambitions both directly and through her agents in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and her military intervention both directly and through her agents in the same state. In respect of the political intervention, I will be very brief. My learned friend, Mr. Kehoe, has already addressed you at some length on this. I think I only need say that Dr. Franjo Tudjman stated both publicly and privately that he had aspirations for the territorial aggrandisement of the Republic of Croatia. Testimony has demonstrated that this dangerous ambition was to be fulfilled by an agreement on the partition of Bosnia-Herzegovina between the Serbs and the Croats. As my learned friend, Mr. Kehoe, has recently said, the Muslims were to be relegated to a small and insignificant element of a Greater Croatian state. The evidence shows, in this case, that this doctrine was transmitted by Zagreb to the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where it was publicly and privately repeated by Mate Boban and his gang of subordinates in Central Bosnia, comprising of Mr. Dario Kordic, who is now residing with us here in The Hague, Mr. Anto Valenta and Mr. Ignac Kostroman. The evidence is overwhelming in this case that the accused, General Blaskic, was tasked with the military facilitation of this policy, and in that respect I would refer you to your own witnesses, Colonel Robert Stewart, [redacted], [redacted]. I would also refer you to Prosecution Brigadier Alistair Duncan and Witness DX who was called for the Defence. Let me now turn to the evidence showing the military intervention of the Republic of Croatia in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is at the heart of the Prosecutor's position on this point. The essence of the Prosecutor's argument is twofold. Firstly, the Prosecutor says that Croatia's overall control and support of the HVO gave rise to an international armed conflict at the time that armed conflict broke out between the HVO and the Bosnian army in May of 1992. Alternatively or in addition to the direct military intervention by the Republic of Croatia and participation of its armed forces on behalf of the HVO in the armed conflict between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina gave rise to an international armed conflict at the latest by January 1993, when units of the Croatian army participated in military operations against the Bosnian army and Bosnian Muslims. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Croats of Bosnia, from early on, looked to Croatia for military support and guidance. On the 21st of March, 1992, the then commander of the Herceg-Bosna Central Bosnia command, Pasko Ljubicic, a character of whom you've heard much in this case, requested by letter a meeting with the Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia, the late Gojko Susak, in order to receive instructions on further actions in the area. I would direct you, in respect of that particular piece of evidence, to Exhibit 406/4, which is in the two volumes of material which were submitted last July and which, if you recall, I did an oral summary of those documents. On the 8th of April, 1992, after President Franjo Tudjman formally recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO was created. Two days after this, President Tudjman appointed General Janko Bobetko to the position of commander of the southern front of the Croatian army in charge of all land and sea forces between Split and Dubrovnik. That is Exhibit 406/6. What is the significance of this appointment in this case? Well, it is this: Within eight days of his appointment and on the 16th of April, 1992, Bobetko established a forward command post of the Croatian army southern front command in Grude in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the first document that you will find in the binder in front of you. Now, I would ask you to review that document with me briefly. One of the points that I would like to make about this document is that you will see in paragraph 2 that General Bobetko appoints as his deputy, the language suggests that it is his deputy, Colonel Milivoj Petkovic. [Redacted], the same witness who you called to testify in this case, who stated that in April of 1992, he left the HV and became a brigadier and chief of staff of the HVO. At this time, [redacted] apparently was still in the HV and was answering directly to General Bobetko. By his order of the 19th of May, 1992, Bobetko had established a Central Bosnia forward command post in Gornji Vakuf. Just over a month later, the accused General Blaskic would command this headquarters, a headquarters established, set up, by a Croatian General who had been appointed to his position by Franjo Tudjman. The establishment of the Central Bosnia forward command post you will find is document 2, is tab 2. Again, if I could ask you briefly to review that document with me, you will see it is issued on headed paper of the Republic of Croatia, Southern Front Command, Split Operative Zone Command, Ploca Forward Command Post. In this order, General Bobetko appoints Brigadier Zarko Tole as commander of the forward command post, and you will recall that the accused in his evidence confirmed that this individual was one of his predecessors in the position of commander of the Central Bosnia regional command. The accused also confirmed that Brigadier Zarko Tole was an HV officer, a member of the Croatian army. To orientate Your Honours, I have produced at tab 3 a diagrammatic representation, a map demonstrating to you the two headquarters that were established by General Bobetko. You will see firstly the forward command post at Grude, Croatian army southern front command, and then you will see above it the Central Bosnia forward command post established at Gornji Vakuf which was to be General Blaskic's first regional command after his time in Kiseljak. I have also marked in for your orientation the towns of Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak. I would briefly draw your attention to tabs 4, 5, and 6 which are orders issued by General Bobetko, a Croatian General, to units of the HVO. In tab 4, you will see that General Bobetko is appointing key officers into the HVO: Zarko Tole, Zeljko Siljeg, characters about whom you have heard during the course of this trial. He makes no secret of the fact that he has command over units of the Croatian Defence Council, because if you look at the B/C/S version of this document, it makes it quite clear. The Croatian Defence Council is issuing orders to what the Defence would have you believe is a completely separate army. Tab 5 is another order, again on divisions of zones of responsibility. The significance of this order is that Major General Ante Roso, who is referred to in paragraph 1, as I will probably demonstrate to you after the lunch break, was a Croatian army officer at the time, apparently serving, as far as this paper would lead you to believe, within the HVO. He had not yet even resigned from the Croatian army when this order was being issued to him. The last order is merely to demonstrate to you that General Bobetko had full control over the HVO and was able to issue orders just as he was able to issue orders to units of the Croatian army, and you will note in this document, tab 6, he is addressing an order to General Slobodan Praljak again as commander within the HVO. You will be surprised to hear after lunch, if you recall, that General Praljak was the Assistant Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. Three of Bobetko's immediate subordinates in the southern front command were HV officers: [Redacted], who acknowledged to you when he was here that he was in the HV from July of 1991 until April of 1992 when he joined the HVO as chief of staff. Not a Bosnian returning to serve in the HVO, a native of Sibenik in Croatia. Slobodan Praljak, an HV officer, served in the HVO from August 1993 until November 1994. As I have already said to you, and this can be seen from tab 7, and it is, in fact, the final paragraph, the penultimate paragraph where it states -- I'm sorry, the final paragraph where it states that the talks were attended by General Major Slobodan Praljak, Deputy Defence Minister. On the 21st of April, 1992, Bobetko ordered the then HV General Ante Roso to the defence of Livno in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you will find that it is not a document that I have incorporated into this bundle but it document 406/11. On the 27th of June, 1992, General Blaskic acknowledged that he was promoted to be commander of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone by Ante Roso who was then a serving Croatian army General. Now, General Blaskic stated to this Tribunal that when he was promoted by Roso, he knew absolutely nothing about General Roso's background or function. Mr. President, Your Honours, armies do not work like that. Officers talk with each other about their background, about where their last posting was. It is inconceivable that the accused did not know that this individual was an HV officer. You might wish to finish at this point because I will need to move into private session in order to address the next set of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, when the Prosecutor asks for going back into public session, can the booth hear this? Because I don't think that the Judges are disputing this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
