utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In April and May of 1992, the then Colonel Blaskic acknowledged that he received approximately ten orders from General Ante Roso, and I submit to you this merely reinforces what I have said already, that the accused lied when he said nothing about Ante Roso's background. Why would he lie? Because he did not wish to place a Croatian army officer in the chain of command in the HVO in April or May of 1992. On the 8th of May, 1992, Ante Roso issued an order banning the Bosnian Territorial Defence forces, the forces of the government in Sarajevo on the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The order further stated that the only legal units within the Croatian community were HVO units. If I can direct your attention to tab 11, which is the order of Ante Roso, you will see I have summarised what that order -- the essence of that order, and I would ask you to note the confidential order number, which is 33192 on that order. If you turn to tab 12, which is an order of the 11th of May, you will see that the accused was issuing an order in almost identical form in response to the order of General Ante Roso. Blaskic does state in his evidence to this Court that at the time there were armed conflicts taking place in the Kiseljak municipality. It's expressed in a somewhat confused form but, nevertheless, there were Muslims and Croats fighting each other during this time period. It is, therefore, our submission that the implementation of the order of the Croatian army General Roso by the then Colonel Blaskic demonstrates that by May of 1992, firstly, that the HVO was controlled by the Croatian army and thus Muslims in HVO controlled territory were in the hands of the Croatian army and the Republic of Croatia; and secondly, that the armed conflict that began in May of 1992 was an international armed conflict between the Republic of Croatia on the one hand and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other hand. I now wish to address Your Honours on the issue of control of the HVO by the Republic of Croatia, and in order to do that we will need to move back into private session. Thank you. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 19 (redacted) 20 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In respect of other evidence showing HVO control, HV control of the HVO, I would refer you to Prosecutor's Exhibit 406, volumes I and II, and a summary of those documents that I gave to the Trial Chamber in July of last year. Now, the Republic of Croatia's involvement in the war was not simply limited to its control of the HVO and the structures of Herceg-Bosna, but it also extended to the deployment of Croatian army units and equipment to fight alongside the HVO against the Bosnian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. By the 15th of May, 1992, there were significant elements of the Croatian army present in Bosnia-Herzegovina. By Resolution 752, the Security Council recognised the presence of large bodies of Croat troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina and called on the Republic of Croatia to withdraw them from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to cease interference in that State. The Republic of Croatia totally ignored this demand. If we could now return to closed session testimony, with your permission, Mr. President. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In addition to all of the evidence that I have referred to, there is a substantial amount of documentary evidence which demonstrates the presence of HV soldiers in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the provision of everything by Croatia, from gasoline to heavy armour, throughout 1992, 1993, and 1994, and I would again refer Your Honours to Volumes I and II of Prosecutor's Exhibit 406. Two documents which I think are worthy of particular note in Prosecutor's Exhibit 600, which I haven't put in the binders in front of you but I will briefly summarise what that exhibit states, in that exhibit, the commander of the HVO brigade in Gornji Vakuf writes to the commander of the 4th Split Brigade of the Croatian army stating that one of their soldiers, Croatian army soldiers, was killed in combat whilst fighting with the HVO brigade in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The next document is Prosecutor's Exhibit 601, which you will find at tab 16 in the file in front of you. Here the commander of the HVO brigade in Gornji Vakuf, Mr. Zrinko Totic, is requesting of the 2nd Brigade of the Croatian army that one of their officers, Mate Kunkic, could remain with the HVO brigade. The letter states that the Croatian officer had been engaged in combat with the Bosnian army and had, in fact, been entrusted with the command of the defence of the town of Gornji Vakuf in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, I don't intend to read the entire request to you, but I would commend it to Your Honours. It certainly shows beyond doubt that there was a very significant interchange of personnel between the Croatian army and the HVO, and certainly the manner that this is set out expresses a common struggle by the Croatian army and the HVO against the Muslims. That is very clear from this document. I would now like to briefly refer to Croatian army presence and participation in Central Bosnia. In order to trigger the provisions of the grave breaches, it is unnecessary for the Prosecutor to demonstrate that Croatian army units were present in Central Bosnia during the critical period of this indictment. Be that as it may, it is my submission that there is evidence, significant evidence, to show that units of the HV were in Central Bosnia and were operating both within and alongside the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (redacted) soldiers wearing HV badges in the Dubravica school. She spoke to one of the members of the unit who stated that they had been specially brought in to "sort out the problems with the Muslims." You will recall the evidence of Dr. Muhamed Mujezinovic who observed soldiers from Croatia in the Vitez health centre in January of 1993. Major Roy Hunter, a company commander with the British Battalion in the summer of 1993. His opinion was that intelligence indicated that Croatian army units were acting together with HVO units in the Lasva Valley. He also confirmed that a Croatian army helicopter was landing in the Vitez area in the summer of 1993, thus ensuring both communications and adequate supplies were coming from the Republic of Croatia. Muslim victims of HVO attacks and forced labour testified in respect of a large number of sightings of HV soldiers, and I would refer you particularly in this respect to Witness R, Abdulah Ahmic, (redacted), Witness Q, and Witness BB. Now, you will recall that General Blaskic has maintained throughout this trial that there were no Croatian army officers or soldiers present in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone. The orders that he issued requesting data on HV officers in his unit he states were only issued because the general staff of the HVO requested that the orders be sent out, and I would refer you to Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/26 and 406/55 in that respect. I have, in fact, included 406/55 as tab 17 in the bundle in front of you, and you will see it is an order by Tihomir Blaskic of the 12th of April, 1993, in which he requests information about Croatian army officers in the units under his command. So, in essence, Mr. President, Your Honours, we are all expected to believe that these orders were transmitted up and down the chain of command in the full knowledge that they had no application to anybody at all. Hard to believe. Hard to believe because it is not true. On the 5th of June, 1992, Gojko Susak, the Defence Minister of the Republic of Croatia, sent 13 members of the 101st Brigade of the Croatian army to the southern front command on temporary assignment. Included in that list were Colonel Miro Andric, Blaz Andric, Mirsad Sivac, and Branko Kozul, and if you go to tab 18 in the bundle of evidence in front of you, you will see that order. On the 3rd of May, 1993, the same Colonel Andric reported back to the HV 101st Brigade that he and the four servicemen that I have referred to were serving with the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna pursuant to the Croatian Defence Minister's order. Colonel Andric at this time represented himself as a member of the HVO staff, the HVO main staff, and you will see, if you go to tab 19, that the report is sent from the town of Vitez and that the stamp on the original document is the stamp of the accused from the Central Bosnian Operative Zone. Now, in his evidence, the accused denied that he knew that Andric was a member of the Croatian army. He stated that he thought he was a member of the HVO command, just like he denied that he knew that Ante Roso was a member of the Croatian army when he was appointed by him. Now, General Blaskic does confirm that Andric was participating in discussions with Petkovic and he with the Bosnian army in Zenica. Prosecutor's Exhibit 607, which is document 20 in the tabulated documents before you, indicates that Mr. Andric went on to greater and grander things in the Croatian army after his service in Central Bosnia, to become a brigadier and later a general in the Croatian army, and in 1997, you will see from this report, this BBC report, in the very last sentence, that he was, in fact, head of the Office for Military Attaches and Protocol within the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia. It is our submission, in addition to my first submission, that by early January 1993, at the latest, Croatian army units had entered Central Bosnia and Bosnia generally, and in conjunction with the HVO, participated then on with HVO units engaged in military operations against the Bosnian army in Central Bosnia and elsewhere. The Republic of Croatia did not advertise the fact that its forces were present and fighting against the Bosnian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. A constant stream of public statements by government officials denying any presence of the Croatian army beyond the Bosnian borders were made, and I would refer you to Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/28, 406/64, and 406/70; 406/70, when Mr. Tudjman and his Defence Minister are denying the presence of Croatian army units except in the borderland areas. The fact that HV personnel were serving in Bosnia-Herzegovina against Bosnian forces was often concealed, as I have said, through the interchanging of military paraphernalia and badges which would identify the unit. On the 3rd of October, 1993, Drazen Gvozden was killed on Mount Hum near Mostar. At his death, he was wearing an HVO uniform. On the 2nd of March, 1994, President Franjo Tudjman posthumously conferred on Mr. Gvozden the rank of reserve captain of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, and I would refer you to Prosecutor's Exhibit 609 to 614 in that respect. Orders are in evidence requiring Croatian army members to remove Croatian army insignia and replace them with HVO insignia, and those are Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/26, 406/31, and 406/36. Admiral Domazet, the chief of Croatian military intelligence, you will recall under cross-examination refused to state the outer deployment of Croatian army units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He did acknowledge to you, Your Honours, that those HV officers, those Croatian army officers who went to Bosnia-Herzegovina to serve in the HVO required approval from the Croatian authorities to do so and continued to be paid by the Croatian government. They had an automatic right to return to the Croatian army after their time in the HVO. That was Admiral Domazet's testimony. Now, the Defence say in their brief that the Prosecutor has not sufficiently met the test set out in the Tadic appeal judgement. Your Honours, we have proved: (1) A unity of political direction and control going right from the top with Franjo Tudjman down to Dario Kordic in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (2) We have proved a Croatian General, Janko Bobetko, established by his own order the regional command of the HVO that General Blaskic himself would command. He appointed Blaskic's predecessor, and that same General, appointed by Franjo Tudjman to his post, demonstrated that he was able to issue military orders to both the HVO and the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. (3) Principal positions in the HVO were held by HV officers. An HV officer, Ante Roso, indeed issued the order banning the Bosnian Territorial Defence in May 1992. Ante Roso appointed Blaskic to his position in the HVO. Croatian army officers who went into the HVO continued to be paid by the Croatian army and had an automatic right to return to the Croatian army. (4) A Defence witness testified in this case that the political leadership in Zagreb not only monitored and controlled the HVO but appointed its military leadership. (5) The Croatian army was fighting with the HVO from May 1992 until February 1994, and specifically with the HVO in the Muslim-Croat war, providing it with manpower, supplies, and equipment. Croatian personnel regularly rebadged into the HVO. Lastly, the accused himself was directly transferred by Franjo Tudjman, commander in chief of the Croatian armed forces, from the HVO to the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, under (4), you refer to a Defence witness who "testified in this case that the political leadership in Zagreb not only monitored and controlled the HVO but appointed its military leadership." Should I take it you have a good reason for not being more explicit about the identity of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I mentioned earlier in my submissions, I think I identified that witness in closed session. In conclusion, Mr. President, Your Honours, it is our submission that in the Muslim-Croat war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republic of Croatia played a full and substantial part which I would ask you to determine as overall control of the HVO, going beyond the mere financing and equipping of such forces but also involving the participation in the planning and supervision of military operations. This, I would suggest to you respectfully, is the only conclusion that can be reached in this case. Now, the second requirement that I stated to you before lunch, and this will be a much shorter submission, is that the grave breaches must be perpetrated against persons and property defined as protected by any of the four Geneva Conventions of 1949, and I will just read the first section of Article 4 of the IV Convention: "Persons protected by the Convention are those who, at a given moment and in any manner whatsoever, find themselves, in case of a conflict or occupation, in the hands of a Party to the conflict or Occupying Power of which they are not nationals." The Defence say in this case that the Bosnian Muslim victims prima facie found themselves in the hands of Bosnian Croats, victims in the hands of perpetrators of the same nationality. Do the Geneva Conventions apply to this situation bearing in mind what I have just read from Article 4? They do, and the appeals judgement in Tadic confirms this position, and I will read the relevant sections of that judgement which I think are applicable. It is three quite small sections. First of all, paragraph 166: "Under these conditions, the requirement of nationality is even less adequate to define protected persons. In such conflicts, not only the text and the drafting history of the Convention but also, and more importantly, the Convention's object and purpose suggest that allegiance to a Party to the conflict and, correspondingly, control by this Party over persons in a given territory, may be regarded as the crucial test." And then I will read two sentences from paragraphs 168 and 169, and these are the final sentence at paragraph 168 and the first sentence at paragraph 169: "In granting its protection, Article 4 intends to look to the substance of the relations, not to their legal characteristics as such. "169. Hence, even if in the circumstances of the case the perpetrators and the victims were to be regarded as -- I think there is a "the" missing. "Hence, even if in the circumstances of the case the perpetrators and the victims were to be regarded as possessing the same nationality, Article 4 would still be applicable." That legal reasoning, Mr. President, Your Honours, applies as much to this case as it does to the Tadic case. I will briefly address the political and military links between the Republic of Croatia and the Bosnian Croats in order to demonstrate this test of allegiance which the Tadic appeals judgement has given to us. As has already been stated, the aspirations of President Tudjman in respect of Bosnian territory were very clear; that these aspirations were shared by the HVO and by Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina is apparent from the evidence and can be seen in Exhibit 406/2 where the Croatian political leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina is reaffirming and supporting the Banovina Plan for Bosnia-Herzegovina. President Tudjman granted Croatian citizenship to Bosnian Croats at the time that Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by the State of Croatia, and that is apparent from Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/2. The Bosnian Croats reacted to this and applied in their hundreds for Croatian citizenship, and that can be seen in Prosecutor's Exhibit 406/47, 406/51, 406/52, 406/59, 406/68, and 406/69. You will recall that Prosecution counsel asked a number of witnesses for the Defence, "What passport do you carry?" Slavko Katava from Busovaca, [redacted], Tomislav Rajic all waved Croatian passports in front of you. If we can now move into private session? I would add, if I'm not being clear, that all of those witnesses were Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Croats of Bosnia-Herzegovina looked to the Republic of Croatia as the land of their fathers. Every policy issued and every statement uttered by the HDZ in Croatia and in Bosnia has encouraged that polarisation and permanent shift of allegiance by the Croats of Bosnia to the Republic of Croatia. I will briefly mention the relationship between the perpetrators and the victims. It hardly needs mentioning in this case that in Central Bosnia, the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims came to regard each other as bitter enemies. When the HVO took Muslims into detention, or beat them, or killed them, or burnt down their villages, those Muslims clearly regarded themselves as being in the hands of a party to a conflict. What did the HVO think of the Muslims. Well, I would briefly refer to Exhibit 406/95, which I have not included in the bundle but I will read it out. It is the minutes of a meeting of the HVO municipalities held in September of 1992, at which the accused General Blaskic, was present on the working presidency. The minutes indicate that he spoke at the meeting -- I'm sorry, it's 456/95. My learned friend, Mr. Kehoe, has just corrected me. These are some of the observations that were made at that meeting: "New refugees are arriving daily, especially Muslims. This could disturb the ethnic balance in our areas. The policy should be such that our municipalities serve as a transit point for Muslim refugees who should be directed to Muslim municipalities. Reception centres for refugees which are planned by the government in Sarajevo on Croatian territories are not acceptable to the Croatian population, because that would mean the disruption of the ethnic balance. If the war is prolonged, such centres would be an Islamic fundamentalist's Trojan horse on Croatian territory. Croatian refugees can be provided for by Croats, without centres. Exiled Bosnia and Herzegovina government and its bodies with pro-Muslim policies are undesirable on our territory and their possible activity contrary to the principles of HDZ bodies shall not be tolerated. There is no Bosnian language and it is an insult to the Croatians when anyone tries to make the Croatian language into some kind of Bosnian language." I wish now to briefly consider with you the enclaves, the Busovaca, Vitez and Kiseljak enclaves as occupied territory within Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions. The Prosecutor also takes the position in this case that the Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak pockets were occupied territory. The British manual of military law, a book I'm very familiar with, in part 3 employs a two-part test to determine when territory is occupied. The first part of the test is this: "Due to the occupation, the legitimate government is no longer able to exercise publicly its authority in the territory concerned." And two: "The invading force, on the other hand, is in a position to control and to enforce its authority in the same territory." The reference to this is contained in book I of the Prosecutor's brief. It is, in fact, paragraph 503 of part 3 of the manual. In this case, the evidence is such that you may determine quite legitimately that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Vitez, Busovaca, and Kiseljak was no longer exercising any reasonable authority during the relevant period of this indictment. The evidence shows in this case that the HVO seized control in all three municipalities. Croatia controlled the HVO and the evidence shows in this case that the HVO both gained and sought control in all of the municipalities that were declared to be part of Herceg-Bosna, and I would refer you back to Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/95, which I have just read from, in which senior HVO officials were discussing the level of control which they exercised in those municipalities which they regarded as Croatian territory. It is our submission that at its highest, the evidence demonstrates that the Muslim victims were in the hands of an occupying power, the Republic of Croatia through its de facto agent the HVO. Even if you were to find, Your Honours, that the territory were not occupied, the evidence demonstrates conclusively that the victims were in the hands of the party to the conflict, the HVO, again as de facto agents of the Republic of Croatia. I will now briefly address you on co-belligerent status and diplomatic relations and how this affects protection afforded under the Geneva Conventions. The protection afforded under the conventions does not extend to civilians in the hands of a State that is allied and has normal diplomatic relationship -- a normal diplomatic relationship with their own State. Now, the Defence has suggested in this case that Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia, during this war, maintained diplomatic relations and were, in fact, co-belligerents against the JNA and the army of Republika Srpska, the VRS. The truth revealed by the evidence in this case is that Croatia adopted a dual Machiavellian policy with Bosnia-Herzegovina. Robert Donia, the historian who testified at the beginning of the case, mentioned this in his lengthy testimony. Where it suited the Republic of Croatia to be in alliance with the government in Sarajevo, it was so. When its interest do not suit it to be in alliance, then it was not. If we could go briefly, and I think almost finally, into private session, please, Mr. President. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness DT then testified himself, in fact, that the 5th Corps in Bihac significantly assisted the defence of Croatia. He confirmed this. Bobetko, in fact, stated that the HV regarded it as a corps behind enemy lines. But let us look at the reality of the war in Central Bosnia. Defence Exhibit 345 is a list of 560 names of dead HVO soldiers killed in combat with the Bosnian army. These are the dead of a war fought out not between co-belligerents but between bitter enemies. In May of 1993, Haso Efendic of the Bosnian government made a public statement on behalf of the government in Sarajevo, and that is contained at tab 22, and I will read out a small section of that statement that was made at the time: "The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina states once again that it wishes to develop all-encompassing relations and cooperation with the Republic of Croatia on the basis of mutual trust and respect. However, unless the attacks are immediately stopped and the units of the State of Croatia are withdrawn immediately from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina will be forced to turn to the International Community and request protection from the aggression." Even Professor Degan, who was brought here by the Defence to state that the relations were, in fact, entirely normal between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, stated that the armed conflict between Croatian soldiers and Bosnian government forces was unlawful armed intervention against the sovereign government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Moreover, Professor Degan acknowledged that had the cutting of supplies and military material occurred by the Republic of Croatia, that would not be the act of a co-belligerent. If we can very briefly go into private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are going to continue now. I wish to say for the benefit of the public that we are in the final week of the trial against General Blaskic, who is here present, and that we are listening to the closing arguments of the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Cayley has finished his part and has left, and it is now Mr. Harmon's turn. We are listening to you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. I would like to, first of all, discuss with Your Honours the HVO in Central Bosnia, and in that respect, I would like to remind the Chamber of the proposition that has been put forth by the Defence to this Chamber that General Blaskic was commanding armed peasants. That is a proposition that has been put before you repeatedly, and it is something that I would like to put into context because it gives the impression that we are not talking about a developed country, a highly industrialised country and a country with a strong military tradition. The former Yugoslavia had compulsory military service for all men of military age, able-bodied, between the ages of 18 and 26, and that compulsory military service lasted a minimum of 12 months; and during those 12 months, the able-bodied men of the former Yugoslavia learned military skills and, more importantly, they learned the principle of subordination because one of the paramount considerations and principles in the JNA was the principle of subordination. The principle of subordination wasn't an alien concept that was brought over and dropped into Central Bosnia; it wasn't the first giraffe that was seen by Western Europeans; it was a concept that was fully and completely understood. If I could have the principle of subordination placed on the ELMO? Mr. President and Your Honours, this was a principle that was immediately engrafted into the decree of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and I will take just a moment to read this. It is found in Article 32, which is in our Exhibit 38, tab 2: "Command in the Armed Forces shall be founded on the following fundamental principles: (a) unity of command and the obligation to implement the decisions and carry out the command and orders of a superior commander; and (b) commanders of the Armed Forces shall be responsible to their superiors for their work, command and control." So this, Mr. President, was a principle that was well understood by virtually -- by everybody who had served in the former JNA. Now, when we talk about JNA, we are talking about an army that was considered by the Western powers, by the NATO alliance, to be one of the most formidable armies and potential foes in Central Europe. It was a large army. We have heard testimony about the size of the army. It was an army that had excellent training. It was an army that had officers who came from military academies, the military academy -- one of them was in Belgrade. General Blaskic graduated from the military academy in Belgrade, other officers in the JNA graduated from the military academy. They also had a reserve officer training programme, and the reserve officer training programme resulted in individuals who didn't go to the military academy being commissioned as officers and being part of this potentially formidable foe, this large army, the JNA. You know, we have had some testimony in this case about the quality of the reserve officer training programme which made up a fundamental part of the JNA officer corps. I got the sense when I was listening to this testimony that the Defence in some way was trying to denigrate the quality of officers that were coming out of that particular programme, and I would like to remind the Trial Chamber, we all come from different countries, but in my country, the United States, not every officer who serves in the military has graduated from Annapolis or has graduated from West Point. There are other ways to become an officer. Those officers who come up through other mechanisms, through other channels, are considered fine officers, they are excellent officers, and they make up the bulk of the United States Army. Likewise, not every officer from the United Kingdom graduates from Sandhurst or, from the French army, graduates from St. Cyr. Reserve officer programmes are fundamental aspects of large militaries, it is a reality, and it was a reality in the former JNA. Now, let me also mention that when the discussion hit upon a peasant army, what we are talking about is a level of training from the JNA that created a vast pool of experience that was available to the HVO, it was available to the ABiH, and it was available to the VRS, and it is not as though the war -- the former Yugoslavia disintegrated, the mandatory service dissolved, and there was a hiatus of 15 or 20 years where the experience level of people who were trained in military elements disappeared, we are talking about a transitional period from the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia, 1991 and 1992, when there was compulsory service, to the beginning of this war which started in 1992 and 1993. So we are not talking about a large gap where military-aged and eligible men for service did not have military training. The conclusion we can draw from the compulsory military service is, there was a large body of available men with training in the military, in military skills, and primarily in the unity of command that was available to all parties in this conflict. We heard some testimony in the course of this trial that the HVO didn't meet NATO standards. Now, let's examine that because it has been conceded in this trial that NATO had the most formidable military services in the world. It has the best-trained officer corps, it has the best armaments, it has the best equipment in terms of communications. What we also heard from Witness DX was the former JNA did not meet NATO standards, and very frankly, most countries that have signed up and have agreed to abide by the Geneva Conventions don't meet NATO standards. That's a red herring. The signatories to the Geneva Conventions, whether or not they meet NATO standards, are still obliged to abide by the provisions of those standards. Let me move on to the next aspect of the HVO that I would like to discuss with you, and that's training. First of all, we have heard Brigadier Marin testify in this case that the level of training in the HVO -- first of all, he said there was none, then he changed his testimony and ultimately he said, in response to a question by my colleague, Mr. Kehoe, and to another question by Judge Shahabuddeen, that the HVO carried out a level of training that was "minimal and most essential." Let's examine what the HVO did in respect of training this large pool of already-trained military men who had done compulsory service. If we could turn to the first exhibit? This first exhibit -- and I won't present all of the exhibits that discuss training -- but this first exhibit that I would like to show is one dated the 10th of May, 1992, and it is an order that was issued by Colonel Blaskic in Kiseljak on the 10th of May, and in point 4, he says: "4. All Municipal HVO Commands must begin with training and additional training of soldiers in locations which must be under guard." So Colonel Blaskic, as soon as he arrived in the theatre, started to train his soldiers. At the same time, we've heard testimony in this case about HOS. HOS was another organisation separate from the HVO. As we've heard, it ultimately evolved into -- it disintegrated and many of the members went into the HVO. But let's take a look at the next exhibit, which is D249. D249 is a report from Major Darko Kraljevic, dated the 19th of July, 1992, to the HOS war staff command in Zagreb. What does Darko Kraljevic have to say about the level of training that's taking place? If we turn to the third paragraph, Kraljevic says in 3: "3. The training camp in Vitez has been in existence for four months now. Five hundred troops have been trained there. Their operations and sabotage actions are the best proof of the quality of training." So in addition to the HVO training that was being initiated by Colonel Blaskic in the Kiseljak municipality, there had been training going on for four months where 500 members had been trained. Moving along, I'd like to turn the Court's attention to Prosecutor's Exhibit 104, because the training that was being given by Colonel Blaskic to his subordinates wasn't limited to basic training. If we turn to Exhibit 104, we can see that this order issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 23rd of July, 1992, deals with specialised training in specialised equipment. In this case it's a Strela artillery piece, and he identifies a large number of soldiers in this particular document that will be trained on this particular occasion in the use of that particular weapon system. If we turn next, Mr. President and Your Honours, to July 24th, 1992, we can see another order of Colonel Blaskic. This one is an order where he is sending his subordinate soldiers to Croatia to be trained. He discusses the needs of those soldiers and what they will be trained in and when they will go. Training was across the board in the HVO, Mr. President and Your Honours, and I'd like to turn next to an exhibit, Prosecutor's Exhibit 484. Now this -- I will only put on the ELMO the cover sheet of this rather lengthy exhibit that we presented, and what this is a training plan and programme for recruits of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It is dated the 1st of September, 1992 and it is issued by Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic. I would commend Your Honours to examine this document, because if in your deliberations -- in your deliberations you will see, by merely looking at the index, the contents of this training programme are extensive. As I recall Brigadier Marin testified, this training programme lasted 22 days and it covers a variety of topics. What is more remarkable about this exhibit, however, is the fact that there's not a single moment of training in International Humanitarian Law, on the laws and customs of war, on the Geneva Conventions. Now, if we move on in this, Mr. President and Your Honours, we can see that in addition to the training that I have described now taking place, there was additional training that was taking place in other parts of, as I say, other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the HVO. I don't have a copy of it here because there are too many exhibits, but I would refer Your Honours to Prosecutor's Exhibit 457, page 17 in that particular document, "Three Years of Military Police History," which there is a report that deals with what we've accomplished in the various -- from January 1993 until June of 1993, and on page 17 you will see that there is a reference to training 2.000 HVO soldiers. In addition, Mr. President and Your Honours, we have presented to Your Honours a film. You may recall it. It was a film taken by a reporter, Dan Damon, and it showed training where these soldiers -- HVO soldiers dressed in combat kit, jumping out of trucks and running around in movement, training with dogs. It is another illustration of the level of training that was being conducted by the HVO. Now, if we move next, Mr. President and Your Honours, to Prosecutor's Exhibit 106. This is an exhibit that is dated the 20th of September, 1992. This is also signed by then Colonel Blaskic, and in item number 3 it says: "3. The training of new recruits who have not yet served in the Yugoslav army is to be basic and specific. Recruit all able-bodied men over 18." This goes to ONO, the operations and training body. Now, who is the training officer for Central Bosnia? Brigadier Marin. And the deadline for this particular training for the neophyte soldiers is indicated, 15 to 30 September, 1992. The next exhibit I'd like to direct the Court's attention to is Prosecutor's Exhibit 107. This is a training schedule signed by Colonel Blaskic, and it discusses, it outlines a training regimen that lasts from 6.00 in the morning until 21.00 in the evening. Once, Mr. President and Your Honours, the conflict commenced, Colonel Blaskic sent a report to his superiors on May the 7th. That's found in Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/32. What did Colonel Blaskic say in that report to Mate Boban, to Bruno Stojic, and to Milivoj Petkovic? He says in point 2: "2. Younger troops, especially in Busovaca, 38 killed and 108 wounded so far, are undergoing special training according to the submitted training plan." So even while the war is -- shortly after its most intense phase, the HVO continues to train its young soldiers. Now, Your Honours have heard a large amount of testimony from third parties, independent observers who were operating in theatre in the Central Bosnia area. One of those individuals was Lieutenant-Colonel Watters, and my colleague, Mr. Kehoe, asked Lieutenant-Colonel Watters the following question: He said: Q Let me ask ... And I'm reading from 3649.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask for that clarification. Would you agree with me when I say the HVO soldiers had been trained militarily either in the former JNA or more recently with the regular Croatian forces? Would you agree with that first statement?" Lieutenant-Colonel Watters responded:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of the commanders I met, I know them to be former JNA officers. I cannot give a personal account of the individual soldiers, sir, I did not talk to them about it, but they were certainly trained by their military commanders. We saw them training. Now, in fact, the next exhibit I'd like to show you is a photograph that was taken by one of the British observers who was in Central Bosnia, and this photograph, he testified, shows young HVO soldiers training. Now, what can we conclude, Mr. President, from this testimony that we have heard that this was only armed peasants? What we can conclude from this about the HVO in Central Bosnia is this: They had a large pool of people to draw from into their service who had compulsory military service, who understood the principle of unity of command, and who continued with ongoing training in the HVO. Now, we heard the next claim that was raised by the Defence and raised by Brigadier Marin, "We had lack of trained officers." Now, Your Honours may recall that the impression that one was left with when listening to Brigadier Marin, was that there were only three trained officers in all of Central Bosnia. It was, frankly, an astonishing proposition. It was a misleading proposition, and you may well recall that my colleague, Mr. Kehoe, spent the better part of half a day of the trial session identifying officers who were in Central Bosnia and asking them about the level of training that they had in -- and they had had before they joined the HVO. I would direct your attention, Your Honours, to the Prosecutor's brief, book II, pages 13 through 15, and you will see, and I will not repeat here, you will see a list of some of those officers who were identified. We did not identify all of the officers who served under Colonel Blaskic, we identified some, and you will see that the training that they had included training at the military academy, training at reserve officer training programmes, and you will see that it's quite comprehensive, this list. The problem in Central Bosnia, Mr. President and Your Honours, wasn't the level of training with the officer corps or the level of training of the lower troops, the problem in Central Bosnia was the problem of leadership, the problem of leadership of Colonel Blaskic, because it was his failure of leadership that led to these crimes in Central Bosnia. His hand-selected commander for the Kiseljak municipality was Mijo Bozic. Mijo Bozic was a military academy graduate from Belgrade, and Mijo Bozic was the officer who issued the illegal order to burn the villages in the Kiseljak municipality. That order was issued while Colonel Blaskic was in Kiseljak. Mato Lucic. Mato Lucic was an active duty JNA officer who led the attack on Svinjarevo. We know what happened to Svinjarevo. In Prosecutor's Exhibit 85, ECMM concluded that there had been ethnic cleansing, and you have heard the testimony of the victims from that area and you have seen the photographs of Svinjarevo, yet Mato Lucic was an active military officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (No interpretation). Continue please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mario Cerkez had had reserve officer training. You may recall the testimony of Colonel Henk Morsink who testified that Mario Cerkez, at a Busovaca joint commission meeting, felt confident enough and comfortable enough to threaten to burn the village of Kruscica to the ground. Let's talk about Ivica Rajic, an active JNA officer. He's been indicted for Stupni Do. He was in Kiseljak when Tulica and Han Ploca were burned to the ground, yet he was an active JNA officer. The problem, Mr. President and Your Honours, wasn't a problem of training, it wasn't a problem of whether there was sufficient officers, the essential problem in this case was leadership, and leadership starts at the top and the top is Colonel Blaskic. The question we have to ask is: What kind of leadership did he provide? We would submit to Your Honours that the leadership he provided was such that it encouraged and promoted his subordinates to engage in criminal conduct because they were absolutely confident in the fact that nothing would happen to them as a result. Mr. President and Your Honours, the next area the Defence raised and said that this was an area that certainly impinged upon Colonel Blaskic's ability to command and control, was the area of communications. I think the characterisation was made that the only thing Colonel Blaskic had was an amateur packet communication system that any amateur could crack, and on the 16th of April, he had two telephones in his headquarters. We are left again with the impression that Colonel Blaskic had very little at his disposal, and again we must put this into context. Mr. Kehoe discussed with you earlier the HVO take-over of the various municipalities. That also included the take-over of JNA facilities and that also included the take-over of the equipment in those facilities, including communications equipment. We have heard testimony from various witnesses that the equipment, if it was shared, wasn't shared equally amongst the HVO and the ABiH. We have submitted a lengthy exhibit to Your Honours, it is Prosecutor's Exhibit 757, and this particular exhibit identifies some of the equipment that was made available to the HVO, the types of communication equipment that was made available to the HVO at various times in the municipalities commanded by Colonel Blaskic, and I would urge Your Honours to examine the 77 entries that are found in portion 3 of this exhibit because this describes the various types of communication that were sent to the HVO, to Blaskic's headquarters, to Kiseljak headquarters, to the Busovaca headquarters, and to other headquarters and other elements of the HVO from the maintenance and repair depot in Travnik, and you will see, on close examination of this particular exhibit, you will see that what was sent was radios, various types of radio equipment, short-range, long-range radios, mobile communications vehicles, telephone communications, antennae, radio relay devices, teleprinters, battery rechargers, field switchboards, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Let's be quite frank on this. Colonel Blaskic got his fair share of this. He didn't limit himself to two telephones. We have also heard testimony that the HVO and the Muslims were aligned against the VRS before their conflict started. How was the HVO communicating with its forces on the front lines against the Serbs before this war started? On April 16th, 1993, did the communications capabilities of the HVO vanish? I don't think so. When Colonel Blaskic said he had two telephones in the Hotel Vitez, that was both false and it was misleading. First of all, we have had the testimony of a number of witnesses, third parties and Defence witnesses, who have testified about what they saw in the Hotel Vitez. I refer Your Honours to the testimony of Major Hunter, who was in the Hotel Vitez on May the 20th. He observed radios in the Hotel Vitez. Major Baggesen, who was an ECMM monitor and who was in the Vitez area when the attacks commenced on the 16th of April, he observed radio antennae coming out of the Hotel Vitez and he actually was in the Hotel Vitez and he saw somebody talking on a radio. Brigadier Zeko, Blaskic's chief of intelligence, said that there was a communications area in the hotel. Now, this testimony, "I only had two telephones," leaves the impression again there was minimal amount of communications capability. Let's again examine reality, and reality is the HVO had a communications centre located a few metres across the plaza at the PTT telephone building, and that communications centre was operational. It was operational before the conflict on the 16th of April and it was operational after the 16th of April. How do we know that? Let me show Your Honours some exhibits, starting with D96, and this is only a sample of these exhibits. If Your Honours examine the orders that were sent out by Blaskic and the replies that were sent in from his subordinates in the field, frequently there was a stamp on the order in the B/C/S language reflecting the date and time and location of the receipt. Let me take Your Honours through just four examples to illustrate my point. D96, you will see, Mr. President and Your Honours, on the B/C/S version that's on the ELMO, you will see a stamp, and that stamp on the upper line says "CV HVO Vitez," which is the communications centre stamp, and this was received on the 27th of January, 1993. If we move to Prosecutor's Exhibit D -- I'm sorry, Defence Exhibit 264, I'll put the English version on, and you will see, on the lower right-hand corner, the translation of the stamp, Croatian Defence Council HVO Vitez Communications Centre dated 15 April 1993 at 0711 hours. Moving to now immediately after the conflict, if we go to Prosecutor's Exhibit 288A, again on the ELMO, Your Honours will see the English translation of the stamp indicating Croatian Defence Council Vitez Communications Centre, 17 April 1993 at 0614 hours in the morning. One last example for Your Honours is 303, it is Defence Exhibit 303. Again, this is the B/C/S version of the stamp. It indicates on the lower left-hand corner again the HVO Communications Centre, dated April 18th, 1993. Mr. President and Your Honours, what we see here is that there was a functional operational communications centre a short distance away from Colonel Blaskic, and when he says "I could only communicate on two telephones," that's misleading and it's false. The next question arises -- we've heard Colonel Blaskic testify about problems with his ability to send secure communications. Again, Mr. President and Your Honours, I commend you to Prosecutor's Exhibit 757, particularly the first portion of that exhibit, because in that first portion of the exhibit, there is a series of documents which show (1) that Colonel Blaskic was receiving coded communications from Mostar. I believe in that exhibit -- there are four exhibits in there, four sample exhibits, where General Petkovic sends Blaskic coded communications. Second of all, in that exhibit there are a number of examples of rudimentary codes that were used by various subordinate units of Colonel Blaskic in Fojnica, for example, I believe there is one from Vares. It is inconceivable that Colonel Blaskic did not use codes when he was fighting the Serbs. He was. He used codes. There were codes as standard operating military procedures. He was aware of them and he used them. Could they encrypt their messages? What do we know about that? We know that Brigadier Marin testified before Your Honours -- now, Brigadier Marin, again, was the chief of intelligence. He had an office or a location in Nova Bila, which was near the British base, and I asked Brigadier Zeko, "Did you have encryption capabilities and could you communicate with encrypted communications to the Hotel Vitez?" He said "Yes." So it is clear, Mr. President and Your Honours, from the equipment that was available to them and the communications centre that was there, that the HVO and Colonel Blaskic had far more communications capabilities than he said in his testimony. Again, I'd like to turn Your Honours' attention to the testimony of -- it was Major Baggesen who testified that when he went to HVO positions on Serb lines, he saw HVO communications officer communicating on a radio with various other radio stations in the HVO radio network. Now, that was when they were fighting the Serbs. Captain Jean-Marc Lanthier, who was a member of the Canadian battalion in Kiseljak, his testimony to Your Honours was the HVO had excellent communications at various HVO headquarters. Colonel Stewart, when he testified, testified that it was easy for the HVO headquarters to pass commands down to subordinate units. Let's examine another facet of the problem of communications, and that is: What did the victims tell Your Honours when they came to this Chamber and related their tragic stories? Many of these victims testified that, in fact, while they observed these actions of the HVO soldiers, they saw them. They saw them with Motorolas. I believe a witness by the name of Sulejman Kavazovic testified that in addition to Motorolas he saw hand-held field telephones that were being used. Now, if we could go briefly into private session, it will be very brief, I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. Mr. Registrar. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I must remind you once again, in view of the fact that a maximum of publicity focuses on this debate and that we must limit to a minimum private sessions to only those witnesses that were under protection. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. That's my mistake. Let's turn to Kiseljak and discuss Kiseljak for just a moment. We have heard testimony from a professional military officer, it was Captain Libert who said that physical separation of command is not unusual. It happened on a number of occasions and he cited examples in the Second World War. Was that a problem for Colonel Blaskic? Let's hear the words of Colonel Blaskic. I will refer Your Honours to Prosecutor's Exhibit 380, and this is what Colonel Blaskic said. He was asked the question:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Kresevo, Kiseljak, and part of Fojnica municipality also controlled by the HVO are also in Central Bosnia but are not connected with the forces of Vitez and Busovaca. How are they holding up? Blaskic -- I will read only a portion of this answer given the time, and I'm reading from midway through his answer:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: ... They are carrying out in a coordinated and organised manner all commands connected with the defence of the people and Croatian territories. This physical separation is not an essential or decisive factor, because we figured out in our planning that the temporary physical separation of these areas could occur. Travnik is the first Operative Group, Kiseljak is the second, Zepce the third, and Sarajevo the fourth. All operative groups are under my command with the chain of leadership and command functions absolutely, without interruption. So Colonel Blaskic agreed with Captain Libert that physical separation did not necessarily pose problems with command. Now, I will not repeat the testimonies of Brigadier-General Duncan or Baggesen or Lanthier, but all of them testified to the effect that the command functioned properly in the Kiseljak municipality, and Blaskic told them that there were no problems with the command, even though there was a physical separation between the Vitez-Busovaca municipality and the Kiseljak municipality. That's what he told them then. What he's telling this Trial Chamber now is different. What he told the Donis reporter in October is different than what he's telling this Chamber now. Now, Mr. President and Your Honours, I'd like to turn first of all to identify some of the units and deal quickly with some of the units, whether Colonel Blaskic commanded and controlled these units. Let's start with the artillery. My colleague, Mr. Kehoe, touched upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're going to another subject, are you? I'm asking you in order to be able to follow you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are you still talking about communications? Yes. Very well. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm now talking about units that were under the command of Colonel Blaskic. I'd like to start with, first of all, the artillery. As I say, my colleague, Mr. Kehoe, touched upon that this morning when he discussed the shelling of Zenica on the 19th of April, 1993. Blaskic himself testified that he commanded the important major artillery pieces in his area of operation. Why? Because artillery assets were precious. The lower commands had mortars, smaller millimetre mortars, they had anti-aircraft pieces, but the big pieces were under Blaskic's control and only he could give orders in respect of those. My colleague mentioned why that's important. In part, the Zenica shelling. Briefly let me put another exhibit on the ELMO. This is Prosecutor's 690, and it relates to Colonel Blaskic's testimony about the 16th of April, 1993. On the 16th of April, as you will recall, Colonel Blaskic testified that he was taken by surprise by this attack on the Hotel Vitez. His artillery was unprepared, and as I recall in his testimony, he was not able to organise any artillery response until approximately 9.00 or 9.30 that morning. Now, let's take a look at what a third-party observer identified? The third-party observer, as you will see on this Exhibit A, says that at 06.45 hours, they noticed the artillery piece, a field gun, started to fire from an area and they give the coordinates. Well, during the testimony of this case those coordinates were identified, and those coordinates were at a quarry known as Mosunj, which housed a 152-millimetre artillery piece that was under the exclusive control of Blaskic. So when Blaskic testified in this Chamber that he didn't start the artillery fire until 9.00, 9.30 on the 16th, he had exclusive control over this artillery piece that started firing at 06.45 hours. I'd like to turn next to a special purpose unit known as Zuti. Did Colonel Blaskic command and control this particular special purpose unit? If I could put before this Chamber the following testimony of Brigadier Marin, who testified at page 13965 and 13966. He said as follows:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Zuti units, the yellow units, was within the composition of the Frankopan Brigade, so it was not a unit organisationally linked to the Defence Ministry or any other institution. It was a unit which, that is to say, a group of 30 individuals who proclaimed themselves to be special purpose units, and they acted within the frameworks of the Frankopan Brigade, just as a company or platoon with the framework -- within the framework of the brigade. So this, according to a Defence witness, puts the Zuti special purpose unit directly into the Frankopan Brigade, and we have heard testimony from Colonel Blaskic that he controlled the brigades. Let's take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 456/37, an order, a command by Colonel Blaskic dated June 19, 1993. In the distribution section of this order it says and I quote: "All the independent units under the command of the HVO 3rd OZ commander," and it lists, among others, the Vitezovi, TURTKO II, and Zuti. Now, let's talk about Zuti. How is this Zuti, this organisation, characterised by the Defence? If I can refer Your Honours to page 19612, a question by my colleague, Mr. Nobilo. The following question:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you remind us please, one of the representatives, you say in a very nice way the members of an armed group, but I would like to say Mafioso groups, you mentioned Zuti. Is it the same Zuti that witnesses from the International Community mentioned who was responsible for hijacking of convoys? Answer by Blaskic:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was. He was one of the bosses in the area. So we have Colonel Blaskic testifying that Zuti, in adopting the characterisation by my colleague Mr. Nobilo, that Zuti was one of the Mafioso bosses in the area. Now, let's discuss Zuti a little bit more in the context of war crimes. You may recall Major Baggesen who testified before this Chamber. Let me relate his testimony, starting at page 1978 and going over to 1979. Major Baggesen answered:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to that area and witnessed two Muslim families forced out of their homes and their houses were given over to Croat families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who forced them out of their houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was an HVO unit. We were able to see that and we were told the commander of this unit had the nickname Zuti.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness this event actually happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Further on down the line:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you complain to about this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On our way back we passed Colonel Blaskic and we complained about this to Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you passed Colonel Blaskic? You passed the Hotel Vitez in Vitez and you went to his headquarters and told him about this incident? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said he was sorry and he would try to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think, because at this time it only seems it's as a minor problem that two families were forced out. This occurred on the 11th of May, according to Major Baggesen. The question is: Assuming this was a Mafioso group, a group that stole from international convoys humanitarian aid and a group that, according to Major Baggesen, evicted Muslims from their homes, did Colonel Blaskic have the military might to suppress this group? Absolutely. And I will refer Your Honours to a testimony of Brigadier General Alastair Duncan who was talking in the context of the Vitezovi but it applies equally to Zuti. Brigadier General Duncan testified that Darko Kraljevic and his knights had a number of about 20 or 30 strong, and the question was put to Brigadier General Duncan:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Blaskic have enough troops under his control to control 20 or 30 men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most certainly. If he wished to stamp out 20 or 30 men, he could have done so easily. The next exhibit I would like to turn Your Honours' attention to is Prosecutor's Exhibit 685 because the leader of the Zuti group was a man by the name of Zarko Andric. What happened to this man who ECMM advised had evicted Muslims from their homes, who Blaskic acknowledged had stolen from international humanitarian aid convoys. What happened to him? Was he punished? Was his group suppressed? The answer is "No" to both of those questions, and the answer can be seen in Prosecutor's Exhibit 685. Zarko Andric was personally appointed by Blaskic to be the assistant commander for the active forces in Central Bosnia on the 4th of July, 1993. Let me turn to another special purposes group very briefly, the Tvrtko II group. This Court has heard testimony from Blaskic that on the 16th of April, at 12.34 in the afternoon, Blaskic personally placed the commander of the Tvrtko unit at the disposal of Mario Cerkez and asked him to assist Cerkez in the assault on Doing Veceriska that was taking place. Yesterday my colleague showed Your Honours pictures again of what happened in Doing Veceriska. The Muslims were driven out, their homes were burned to the ground. One of the participating units beside the brigade that was under Blaskic's control was this special purposes unit, and again, if there is any question as to whether this special purposes unit was under Blaskic's control, I would refer Your Honours to 456/37. I have referred to it earlier. The next group is in Kiseljak, special purposes unit known as the Maturice. This was a group, Mr. President and Your Honours, that was part of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, and as such, by Blaskic's own admission that he controlled the brigades, he controlled, obviously, the actions of this particular group. Lastly, I would like to turn to the Vitezovi because Blaskic tried mightily to distance himself from the Vitezovi special purposes unit. What he testified and what Marin testified about was that the Vitezovi was led by Darko Kraljevic, and in order to give Darko Kraljevic an order, an assignment, even after he had been "attached," he would have to negotiate with Darko Kraljevic, and only if Darko Kraljevic agreed could Blaskic rely on the services of the Vitezovi. He also testified that the Vitezovi was out of control and that Blaskic complained all the time to the main staff about the Vitezovi, about their actions, about the actions of their commander, Darko Kraljevic, and that, Your Honours, was a lie. Absolutely a lie. Why did he lie about that? It is quite clear why he did: Because virtually every crime in this indictment has the fingerprints of the Vitezovi on it. I refer Your Honour to a protected witness I referred to a few moments ago who discussed communications while in Ahmici and in the January attack in Busovaca. I won't identify him in public session, but he identifies the Vitezovi as participating in the January attack where the Muslims' houses were burned, where they were attacked, where they were driven out. The truck bomb. We have heard Colonel Blaskic testify that the Vitezovi were the group that was responsible. We have heard testimony of Blaskic saying that the Vitezovi were assigned to guard around his headquarters. We have heard testimony of victims who testified about what happened to the Muslim homes around the Hotel Vitez: They were burned to the ground, civilians were driven out. There is testimony of what they did through third party British officers who drove into Vitez and observed the one-sided combat taking place. The Vitezovi held prisoners at the Dubravica school from the 16th of April until early May, and I would refer Your Honours to the testimony of Dr. Fuad Zeco who testified that the Vitezovi threatened to kill the prisoners in the Dubravica school if the ABiH, in their counterattack, came closer and continued to advance on Vitez. The Vitezovi has been identified in Ahmici as participating in the killings and the burning in Ahmici. My colleague discussed the attack on Stari Vitez on July 18th. Blaskic says, "The Vitezovi did it. I was in Busovaca. I was at breakfast -- I was at mass and I had lunch with the minister." They were identified in Grbavica in September. The point is that everywhere there is a crime, the Vitezovi have their fingerprints firmly on the crime. But Blaskic now needs to distance himself from the Vitezovi. Darko Kraljevic is dead. He can't respond to the claims that Darko Kraljevic was somebody that was out of control. The Prosecutor submits to Your Honours that Blaskic controlled and commanded this particular special purpose unit throughout the war, and they were subordinated to him, they weren't attached to him. You may recall, Your Honours -- if we may have the next exhibit? -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 666, which is an order from Milivoj Petkovic, dated the 19th of January, 1993, and it subordinates the Vitezovi to Colonel Blaskic. It forbids any independent action by that group, and it says: "This order shall remain in force until I personally change it." This is dated the 19th of January, 1993. Now, if we could go into private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, because you are referring to a testimony which is under protection, so we will go into private session, please. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are adjourning now. It is 5.30. We will resume tomorrow at 10.00. I am reminding you that you should finish tomorrow. That is an imperative. Are we agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, we are agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.
